Fix it before treating a failed task as evidence about model quality.</p> <h2 id="privacy-and-team-fit"> <a href="#privacy-and-team-fit" title="Privacy and Team Fit">Privacy and Team Fit</a> <a href="#privacy-and-team-fit" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Privacy and Team Fit">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>A local interface does not establish local inference.</strong> Map the services receiving source code, prompts, tool output, and session data. A local model reduces reliance on remote inference, but connected tools, web requests, plugins, and sharing features still need their own review.</p> <p><strong>OpenCode’s source availability helps inspection and customization.</strong> It also leaves you responsible for evaluating your chosen providers and configuration. Claude Code’s documented managed permission policies and cloud deployment routes offer an alternative for teams standardizing access. Neither software license, by itself, establishes your organization’s data policy.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Team requirement</th> <th>Evaluation question</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Model selection</strong></td> <td>Which approved providers and models must work?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Data handling</strong></td> <td>Where do prompts, logs, and tool outputs go?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Access control</strong></td> <td>Who sets policy, and who has authority to change it?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Operations</strong></td> <td>Who maintains local runtimes and custom integrations?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Review</strong></td> <td>Who approves dependencies, patches, and deployments?</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="run-a-fair-trial"> <a href="#run-a-fair-trial" title="Run a Fair Trial">Run a Fair Trial</a> <a href="#run-a-fair-trial" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Run a Fair Trial">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Start from the same repository revision</strong> in separate disposable branches or worktrees. Use the same instructions, acceptance tests, time limit, and approval policy. If model or serving settings differ, record the difference instead of calling the result an isolated agent comparison.</p> <p><strong>Use tasks with independent checks.</strong> Select a bug with a known reproduction, a small feature with prewritten acceptance criteria, and a refactor protected by existing tests. Let each agent work without seeing the other’s patch. Review both diffs after the task ends.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Measure</th> <th>Record for each attempt</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Correctness</strong></td> <td>Existing tests plus independent acceptance checks</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Time</strong></td> <td>Start to reviewed, usable patch</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Interventions</strong></td> <td>Clarifications and manual repairs</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Change scope</strong></td> <td>Unrelated edits and dependency churn</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Cost</strong></td> <td>Billed usage or local resource cost</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Recovery</strong></td> <td>Response to failed tests and rejected commands</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Repeat the trial before choosing.</strong> One successful task is weak evidence for broad superiority. Generated tests also need review, since an agent sometimes repeats the same mistaken assumption in its implementation and tests. Keep failed attempts in the record.</p> <p><strong>Separate speed from completion.</strong> Fast token generation does not measure test execution, repeated reasoning, or human review. For local configurations, distinguish initial prompt processing from cached continuation. A fast continuation in a warm session does not establish cold-start performance.</p> <h2 id="troubleshooting"> <a href="#troubleshooting" title="Troubleshooting">Troubleshooting</a> <a href="#troubleshooting" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Troubleshooting">#</a> </h2> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Symptom</th> <th>Next check</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Unexpected invoice</strong></td> <td>Active account, API credentials, and provider route</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Ignored project rules</strong></td> <td>File precedence, working directory, and loaded instructions</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Broken tool calls</strong></td> <td>Model capability and serving API compatibility</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Excessive approval prompts</strong></td> <td>Narrow permission rules for known commands</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Slow local sessions</strong></td> <td>Memory pressure, context length, and inference configuration</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Tests pass, behavior fails</strong></td> <td>Independent reproduction and acceptance criteria</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="which-should-you-choose"> <a href="#which-should-you-choose" title="Which Should You Choose?">Which Should You Choose?</a> <a href="#which-should-you-choose" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Which Should You Choose?">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Start with OpenCode</strong> if switching providers or inspecting the agent’s source is central to your workflow. Expect to own more of the decisions about model selection, serving compatibility, and inference costs.</p> <p><strong>Start with Claude Code</strong> if your priority is Anthropic’s integrated experience and you already have suitable Claude access. Evaluate its interfaces, permissions, and organizational deployment options against your team’s requirements.</p> <p><strong>Keep the decision reversible.</strong> Store project rules and acceptance tests in the repository. Review the diff regardless of the agent. Choose using repeated results from your own tasks, then revisit the choice when your model, workload, or billing arrangement changes.</p> <p><strong>Next steps:</strong> The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="local OpenCode and Strata guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/strata-opencode-local-coding-agent-16gb/"> <a href="/articles/strata-opencode-local-coding-agent-16gb/" rel="follow me" >local OpenCode and Strata guide</a> </span> examines a reported consumer-GPU setup. The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="OpenRouter provider comparison"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/openrouter-provider-routing-quality-cost/"> <a href="/articles/openrouter-provider-routing-quality-cost/" rel="follow me" >OpenRouter provider comparison</a> </span> explains why serving endpoints affect context, parameters, and cost even when the model name stays the same.</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Which Local AI Model Should You Run? A GPU Context and Coding Guide for October 2026
item.category: "Local AI" , "AI Hardware" , "Self-Hosted AI" , "GPU Benchmarking" , "Developer Tools" , "AI Economics"
item.description: A practical October 2026 guide to choosing local AI models for coding agents. Compare GPU memory, KV-cache growth, context size, quantization quality, prompt processing, reasoning settings, and cloud rental costs.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>The best local coding model is the one which keeps enough of your project in memory and reads it fast enough to stay useful.</strong> Model size still matters, but a model which fits only after spilling into system RAM often feels worse than a smaller model with a stable context window.</p> <p><em>Choose the model and the memory budget together. Do not choose a model from a tier list, then force it onto unsuitable hardware.</em></p> <p>This guide focuses on coding agents, not short autocomplete prompts. An agent reads files, tool output, compiler errors, and test results before it writes a fix. Those inputs consume context, and context changes the hardware decision.</p> <h2 id="the-video-is-a-reference"> <a href="#the-video-is-a-reference" title="The Video Is a Reference">The Video Is a Reference</a> <a href="#the-video-is-a-reference" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Video Is a Reference">#</a> </h2> <p>The following video compares local models across several GPU memory tiers. It is useful for its practical model-selection observations and reported hardware results. This article takes a separate path by organizing the decision around memory behavior, agent context, prompt processing, and total ownership cost.</p> <script> function loadLiteYouTubeScript() { if (document.querySelector('script[src^="/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js"]')) { console.log('Lite YouTube script is already loaded.'); return; } var scriptTag = document.createElement('script'); scriptTag.src = '/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js'; scriptTag.setAttribute('defer', ''); scriptTag.setAttribute('type', 'module'); scriptTag.setAttribute('fetchpriority', 'low'); document.body.appendChild(scriptTag); } document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { if (typeof yieldToMain === 'function') { yieldToMain(loadLiteYouTubeScript, "user-visible"); } else { loadLiteYouTubeScript(); } }); </script> <style scoped> .lite-youtube-fallback { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; flex-direction: column; gap: 1em; padding: 1em; background-color: #000; color: #fff; text-decoration: none; } .lite-youtube-fallback::before { display: block; content: ''; border: solid transparent; border-width: 2em 0 2em 3em; border-left-color: red; } .lite-youtube-fallback:hover::before { border-left-color: #fff; } .lite-youtube-fallback:focus { outline: 2px solid red; } </style><div itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/VideoObject http://schema.org/LearningResource" style="position: relative; padding-bottom: 56.25%; height: 0; overflow: hidden;"> <meta itemprop="name" content="I Tested Every Local AI Model So You Don't Have To"> <meta itemprop="description" content="A practical comparison of local AI models across GPU memory tiers, with attention to coding workloads and hardware limits."> <meta itemprop="thumbnailUrl" content="https://img.youtube.com/vi/C9M6iUFtVB4/maxresdefault.jpg"> <meta itemprop="contentUrl" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C9M6iUFtVB4"> <meta itemprop="learningResourceType" content="Concept Overview"> <meta itemprop="educationalLevel" content="High school (US)"> <lite-youtube videoid="C9M6iUFtVB4" videotitle="I Tested Every Local AI Model So You Don't Have To" videoplay="" nocookie posterloading="lazy" loading="lazy" params=""> <noscript> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C9M6iUFtVB4" class="lite-youtube-fallback" style="position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; height: 100%; border:0;" title="I Tested Every Local AI Model So You Don't Have To"> <span class="lyt-visually-hidden"></span> </a> </noscript> </lite-youtube> </div> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": ["VideoObject", "LearningResource"], "name": "I Tested Every Local AI Model So You Don\u0027t Have To", "description": "A practical comparison of local AI models across GPU memory tiers, with attention to coding workloads and hardware limits.", "thumbnailUrl": ["https:\/\/img.youtube.com\/vi\/C9M6iUFtVB4\/maxresdefault.jpg"], "contentUrl": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C9M6iUFtVB4", "learningResourceType": "Concept Overview", "educationalLevel": "High school (US)" } </script> <h2 id="why-tier-lists-fail"> <a href="#why-tier-lists-fail" title="Why Tier Lists Fail">Why Tier Lists Fail</a> <a href="#why-tier-lists-fail" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Why Tier Lists Fail">#</a> </h2> <p>A model tier list usually maps parameter count to a GPU memory number. The shortcut is useful for a first estimate. It stops being useful once a coding agent starts reading a real repository.</p> <p>The model weights are the first allocation. The <strong>KV cache</strong> is the growing allocation. It stores attention keys and values for the active context so the runtime does not recompute the entire prompt after every generated token.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Memory consumer</th> <th>What it holds</th> <th>Why it matters</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Model weights</strong></td> <td>The quantized parameters</td> <td>A one-time loading requirement</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>KV cache</strong></td> <td>Notes from the active context</td> <td>Grows as the prompt and conversation grow</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Runtime buffers</strong></td> <td>Temporary computation space</td> <td>Varies by backend and batch size</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Agent instructions</strong></td> <td>System prompts and tool definitions</td> <td>Uses context before project files arrive</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>A model file which fits the card is not proof of a usable agent.</strong> The runtime needs room for the cache, temporary buffers, tool definitions, and the next response.</p> <h2 id="context-is-the-real-budget"> <a href="#context-is-the-real-budget" title="Context Is the Real Budget">Context Is the Real Budget</a> <a href="#context-is-the-real-budget" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Context Is the Real Budget">#</a> </h2> <p>Coding agents spend context on more than source files. The budget also includes system instructions, tool schemas, directory listings, shell output, compiler messages, test results, and prior conversation turns.</p> <p>Three MCP connections with verbose tool definitions often consume several thousand tokens before the agent opens a project file. A small default context then leaves little room for code. The agent still responds, but it loses the working set needed for multi-step repairs.</p> <h3 id="a-simple-context-record"> <a href="#a-simple-context-record" title="A Simple Context Record">A Simple Context Record</a> <a href="#a-simple-context-record" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="A Simple Context Record">#</a> </h3> <p>Before comparing GPUs, record these values:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Project size:</strong> files and approximate source lines in a normal task.</li> <li><strong>Tool overhead:</strong> system prompt, MCP schemas, shell tools, and editor instructions.</li> <li><strong>Error payload:</strong> normal compiler and test output length.</li> <li><strong>Target context:</strong> the largest prompt you want to keep without truncation.</li> <li><strong>Response allowance:</strong> space reserved for the planned patch and explanation.</li> </ul> <p>Use the result as a workload specification. A developer who edits one file at a time has a different memory requirement from a developer who asks an agent to trace an API across a monorepo.</p> <h2 id="kv-cache-changes-the-ranking"> <a href="#kv-cache-changes-the-ranking" title="KV Cache Changes the Ranking">KV Cache Changes the Ranking</a> <a href="#kv-cache-changes-the-ranking" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="KV Cache Changes the Ranking">#</a> </h2> <p>Two models with similar parameter counts often have different context costs. A dense model with every layer contributing to the growing cache often needs more memory than a model using a hybrid attention design.</p> <p>One 27B coding model discussed in the reference material uses a limited set of full attention layers while other layers use a fixed-size summary. The reported 128K context cost stays below 9GB for the cache. A similarly sized model with full growing attention across every layer reportedly needs more than 21GB at the same context length.</p> <p>These figures describe specific model architectures and runtime settings. Treat them as a reason to inspect the architecture, not as a universal memory formula.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Model behavior</th> <th>Context effect</th> <th>Hardware implication</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Full attention at every layer</strong></td> <td>Large cache growth</td> <td>Needs more memory for long prompts</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Hybrid or sliding attention</strong></td> <td>Lower cache growth in some layers</td> <td>More context headroom at the same model size</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Mixture of experts</strong></td> <td>Fewer active parameters per token</td> <td>Lower compute per token, but total weights still need storage</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Long-context extension</strong></td> <td>Larger working window</td> <td>More cache memory and more prompt-processing work</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Read the model architecture before buying memory.</strong> Parameter count alone hides the cost of a long coding session.</p> <h2 id="choose-by-gpu-memory-tier"> <a href="#choose-by-gpu-memory-tier" title="Choose by GPU Memory Tier">Choose by GPU Memory Tier</a> <a href="#choose-by-gpu-memory-tier" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Choose by GPU Memory Tier">#</a> </h2> <h3 id="four-to-eight-gb"> <a href="#four-to-eight-gb" title="Four to Eight GB">Four to Eight GB</a> <a href="#four-to-eight-gb" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Four to Eight GB">#</a> </h3> <p>Small dense models remain the practical choice. They fit the card, respond quickly, and work well for autocomplete, short explanations, and narrow file edits.</p> <p>A larger model with CPU offload might produce text, but response time often becomes the limiting factor. A coding agent needs repeated file reads and tool calls. A four-token-per-second setup turns each repair into a long wait, even when the model technically runs.</p> <p>Mixture-of-experts models offer another path. A small active portion reduces compute pressure, while the full weight set still lives partly in system memory. This approach rewards a system with ample RAM and fast transfer paths.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Workload</th> <th>Suggested direction</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Autocomplete</strong></td> <td>Small dense model with a short prompt</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Single-file edits</strong></td> <td>Small instruct model with tool support</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Repository-wide agent</strong></td> <td>Rent a larger GPU or increase system memory first</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Private code under an NDA</strong></td> <td>Use a local model, but accept a smaller scope or slower runs</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>At this tier, buy system RAM before chasing a large model.</strong> A stable small model beats a large model which spends most of its time moving data across the bus.</p> <h3 id="twelve-to-sixteen-gb"> <a href="#twelve-to-sixteen-gb" title="Twelve to Sixteen GB">Twelve to Sixteen GB</a> <a href="#twelve-to-sixteen-gb" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Twelve to Sixteen GB">#</a> </h3> <p>This tier opens the door to a 27B coding model, but quantization choice becomes central. A standard 4-bit build near 17GB does not fit on a 16GB card once runtime overhead enters the picture.</p> <p>A 3-bit build near 13GB leaves more room for context. A 12GB card pushes the choice toward a 2-bit build or a smaller mixture-of-experts model. Quality depends on the specific quantizer and calibration process, so two uploads with the same bit depth often produce different coding results.</p> <p>Check the following before downloading a quantized model:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Quantizer author and release notes</strong></li> <li><strong>Calibration data and evaluation results</strong></li> <li><strong>Tokenizer compatibility</strong></li> <li><strong>Tool-calling tests</strong></li> <li><strong>Context length at the chosen quantization</strong></li> <li><strong>Runtime support in Ollama, llama.cpp, or the selected front end</strong></li> </ul> <p><strong>Do not treat “2-bit” or “3-bit” as a complete quality description.</strong> The packing method and calibration record matter.</p> <h3 id="twenty-four-to-thirty-two-gb"> <a href="#twenty-four-to-thirty-two-gb" title="Twenty-four to Thirty-two GB">Twenty-four to Thirty-two GB</a> <a href="#twenty-four-to-thirty-two-gb" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Twenty-four to Thirty-two GB">#</a> </h3> <p>This is the most flexible range for a 27B coding model. A 24GB card often fits a 4-bit build with a useful context, but a full 128K window might exceed the remaining memory. A 32GB card gives the runtime more room for the cache and temporary allocations.</p> <p>This range also makes ownership easier to justify. One GPU handles the workload without the complexity of a two-card split. The system uses less power than a multi-GPU build, and software support is easier to test.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Capacity</th> <th>Practical position</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>24GB</strong></td> <td>Strong 4-bit model with context limits to measure</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>32GB</strong></td> <td>4-bit or 6-bit 27B model with broader context headroom</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>48GB</strong></td> <td>Higher precision or larger cache, without changing the core model</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>The 24GB to 32GB range is the sensible ownership zone for frequent private coding work.</strong> It avoids the weakest offload behavior without forcing data-center hardware into a desktop case.</p> <h3 id="forty-eight-gb-and-above"> <a href="#forty-eight-gb-and-above" title="Forty-eight GB and Above">Forty-eight GB and Above</a> <a href="#forty-eight-gb-and-above" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Forty-eight GB and Above">#</a> </h3> <p>More memory does not automatically mean a new model. The same 27B model might run at 8-bit precision on a 48GB card, with a larger cache and fewer compromises. The improvement is consistency, context room, and output quality rather than a new level of reasoning.</p> <p>At 128GB, the decision changes. A much larger mixture-of-experts model becomes possible, but prompt processing becomes a serious concern. A model often generates quickly while taking a long time to ingest a large repository or a fresh tool result.</p> <p><strong>For large models, measure prefill speed separately from decode speed.</strong> A fast answer after a slow prompt read still feels slow in an agent workflow.</p> <h2 id="decode-speed-is-only-half-the-test"> <a href="#decode-speed-is-only-half-the-test" title="Decode Speed Is Only Half the Test">Decode Speed Is Only Half the Test</a> <a href="#decode-speed-is-only-half-the-test" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Decode Speed Is Only Half the Test">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Decode speed</strong> measures generated tokens per second. It answers, “How fast does the model write?” <strong>Prefill speed</strong> measures prompt processing. It answers, “How fast does the model read?”</p> <p>An agent spends much of its time reading. Every tool call adds new text. A long source file, stack trace, or test log enters the prompt before the next response begins.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Metric</th> <th>User experience</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Decode tokens per second</strong></td> <td>How quickly the answer appears after processing</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Prompt tokens per second</strong></td> <td>How long the agent waits before the answer starts</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Time to first token</strong></td> <td>The combined delay from prompt processing and setup</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Context retention</strong></td> <td>How much project state remains available during the task</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Benchmark your own prompt sizes.</strong> A short synthetic prompt hides the cost which matters most during repository work.</p> <h2 id="free-runtime-settings-first"> <a href="#free-runtime-settings-first" title="Free Runtime Settings First">Free Runtime Settings First</a> <a href="#free-runtime-settings-first" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Free Runtime Settings First">#</a> </h2> <p>Hardware upgrades are not the first performance step. Test runtime settings before opening a shopping page.</p> <h3 id="multi-token-prediction"> <a href="#multi-token-prediction" title="Multi-Token Prediction">Multi-Token Prediction</a> <a href="#multi-token-prediction" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Multi-Token Prediction">#</a> </h3> <p>Some model and backend combinations support predicting several future tokens, then verifying them in one pass. The feature is often exposed through a runtime flag or a compatible draft setup.</p> <p>Reported tests in the reference material show large gains on some high-end cards. Results vary by model file, backend, driver, and card. Apple Metal paths might not preserve the required feature during conversion.</p> <h3 id="reasoning-level"> <a href="#reasoning-level" title="Reasoning Level">Reasoning Level</a> <a href="#reasoning-level" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Reasoning Level">#</a> </h3> <p>A model shipped with maximum reasoning enabled spends more time on internal work before returning a result. Medium reasoning often gives a better balance for code repair, especially when the task already includes a clear error message and a narrow file target.</p> <p>Use a simple test matrix:</p> <ol> <li>Run the same bug-fix task with low, medium, and high reasoning.</li> <li>Record time to first token, total time, patch success, and test result.</li> <li>Repeat with a short prompt and a repository-sized prompt.</li> <li>Keep the setting which produces the best completed task, not the highest token rate.</li> </ol> <p><strong>Medium reasoning with a compatible multi-token path is a strong starting point.</strong> Verify quality on your own code before making it the default.</p> <h2 id="local-hardware-or-rental-gpu"> <a href="#local-hardware-or-rental-gpu" title="Local Hardware or Rental GPU?">Local Hardware or Rental GPU?</a> <a href="#local-hardware-or-rental-gpu" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Local Hardware or Rental GPU?">#</a> </h2> <p>Rental compute wins for occasional work. You pay for active sessions instead of buying, cooling, updating, and powering a card all year.</p> <p>Owned hardware wins when the workload is frequent, private, or offline. It also removes queue time and gives you a stable environment for repeatable tests.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Situation</th> <th>Better first move</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>A few sessions per month</strong></td> <td>Rent a GPU or use an API</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Daily private coding</strong></td> <td>Buy a supported 24GB to 32GB system</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Large repository with frequent reloads</strong></td> <td>Rent first and measure prefill speed</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>No code leaves the building</strong></td> <td>Own the smallest system which meets the context target</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Experimenting with a new model</strong></td> <td>Rent before purchasing hardware</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Calculate break-even with active hours, not calendar hours. Include electricity, storage, cooling, maintenance, and the time required to keep the runtime working.</p> <p><strong>A high-end GPU bought for occasional experimentation is a hobby expense.</strong> A 24GB to 32GB system used daily for private work has a stronger economic case.</p> <h2 id="a-better-buying-checklist"> <a href="#a-better-buying-checklist" title="A Better Buying Checklist">A Better Buying Checklist</a> <a href="#a-better-buying-checklist" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="A Better Buying Checklist">#</a> </h2> <p>Use this order when comparing a model and a GPU:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Define the task.</strong> Autocomplete, single-file repair, repository agent, or long-context analysis.</li> <li><strong>Measure the prompt.</strong> Count normal system instructions, tool schemas, files, and test output.</li> <li><strong>Inspect cache behavior.</strong> Look for architecture notes and context-memory measurements.</li> <li><strong>Choose a quantization.</strong> Check quality results from the specific upload, not only its bit count.</li> <li><strong>Test prefill and decode.</strong> Use prompts from your own repository.</li> <li><strong>Tune reasoning.</strong> Compare completed task time at several reasoning levels.</li> <li><strong>Test privacy and maintenance.</strong> Confirm where source code travels and who maintains the backend.</li> <li><strong>Compare rental cost.</strong> Use expected active hours and include power in the owned-system estimate.</li> </ol> <h2 id="final-recommendation"> <a href="#final-recommendation" title="Final Recommendation">Final Recommendation</a> <a href="#final-recommendation" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Final Recommendation">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Under 12GB, run a smaller model or a mixture-of-experts model with enough system RAM.</strong> Do not force a 27B dense model into a setup which spends most of its time offloading.</p> <p><strong>From 12GB to 16GB, focus on quantization quality and a controlled context target.</strong> A well-tested 2-bit or 3-bit build with tool support is more useful than a 4-bit file which never fits cleanly.</p> <p><strong>From 24GB to 32GB, a 27B coding model becomes the practical default for private daily work.</strong> Measure context usage and prompt speed before assuming the full advertised window is available.</p> <p><strong>At 48GB and above, spend the extra memory on precision, cache room, and stable sessions before moving to a larger model.</strong> Once the model crosses into 128GB territory, prompt-reading speed and rental economics deserve more attention than raw capacity.</p> <p>The model name is only the starting point. The useful question is how much project context remains after the model, runtime, tools, and cache take their share.</p> <h2 id="related-reading"> <a href="#related-reading" title="Related Reading">Related Reading</a> <a href="#related-reading" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Related Reading">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="32GB VRAM for Qwen 27B: The Local AI Hardware Guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/32gb-vram-qwen-27b-hardware-guide/"> <a href="/articles/32gb-vram-qwen-27b-hardware-guide/" rel="follow me" >32GB VRAM for Qwen 27B: The Local AI Hardware Guide</a> </span> , focused on hardware paths for a 27B workload.</li> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Llama 3.1 8B and Qwen3.8 27B GPU Benchmarks on Vast.ai"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/qwen38-27b-vast-ai-gpu-benchmark/"> <a href="/articles/qwen38-27b-vast-ai-gpu-benchmark/" rel="follow me" >Llama 3.1 8B and Qwen3.8 27B GPU Benchmarks on Vast.ai</a> </span> , measured rental-GPU results and long-context limits.</li> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Local AI in 2026: A 27B Model Beats Sonnet 4.6"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/local-ai-2026-build-your-rig-now/"> <a href="/articles/local-ai-2026-build-your-rig-now/" rel="follow me" >Local AI in 2026: A 27B Model Beats Sonnet 4.6</a> </span> , model quality, quantization, and local hardware economics.</li> </ul> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: OpenRouter Provider Routing: Model Quality, Token Limits, and Real Costs
item.description: Diagnose inconsistent OpenRouter answers, compare endpoint limits and caching costs, and configure provider routing without disabling quality controls by accident.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>OpenRouter provider routing</strong> affects which inference service answers your request. Two calls using the same model name still depend on endpoint limits, supported parameters, serving software, and routing preferences. When answers become shorter or tool calls fail, check those differences before blaming quantization.</p> <h2 id="key-takeaways"> <a href="#key-takeaways" title="Key Takeaways">Key Takeaways</a> <a href="#key-takeaways" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Key Takeaways">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Precision labels</strong> describe a numerical format, not an accuracy score.</li> <li><strong>Endpoint limits</strong> determine available context, output length, and feature support.</li> <li><strong>Explicit routing</strong> needs a fallback policy as well as a provider preference.</li> <li><strong>Auto Exacto</strong> improves provider selection using quality signals, with an opt-in route for requests without tools.</li> <li><strong>Effective cost</strong> includes output, cache behavior, retries, and successful task completion.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Prerequisites:</strong> Familiarity with JSON requests and access to your application’s OpenRouter configuration. Endpoint inspection uses a public API. Sending model requests requires an API key and incurs usage charges.</p> <p><strong>Time and difficulty:</strong> About 20 minutes for an initial configuration review. Intermediate. A useful comparison across providers requires additional testing with representative prompts.</p> <h2 id="what-your-model-name-omits"> <a href="#what-your-model-name-omits" title="What Your Model Name Omits">What Your Model Name Omits</a> <a href="#what-your-model-name-omits" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Your Model Name Omits">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>A model identifier</strong> selects the requested model. The provider runs the inference service, including its model implementation, token limits, and tool-call parser. A model-level benchmark does not validate every service hosting those weights.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Endpoint property</th> <th>What to check</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Context length</strong></td> <td>Space for the prompt, history, tool results, and generation</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Maximum completion length</strong></td> <td>Output allowance for the requested task</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Supported parameters</strong></td> <td>Tool use, structured output, sampling, and reasoning controls</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Quantization</strong></td> <td>Reported format compared with the original release</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Pricing</strong></td> <td>Input, output, cache reads, and applicable additional charges</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Serving behavior</strong></td> <td>Completion quality, parsing errors, latency, and retries</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Baseline routing</strong> favors lower prices among healthy candidates. OpenRouter documents inverse-square price weighting: in its simplified example, a $1 candidate receives nine times the selection weight of a $3 candidate. This describes relative weights, not a guarantee about your next request. Explicit ordering, sorting, caching, and quality routing also affect selection. See the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="provider routing documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection"> <a href="https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >provider routing documentation</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Price weighting</strong> does not establish the cheapest bill for your workload. The documented example does not specify a universal input/output mixture for its price scalar. Avoid inferring a provider’s selection probability from input price alone.</p> <h2 id="read-precision-in-context"> <a href="#read-precision-in-context" title="Read Precision in Context">Read Precision in Context</a> <a href="#read-precision-in-context" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Read Precision in Context">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Quantization</strong> stores numerical values using a reduced representation. Its effect depends on the model, method, and inference implementation. Lower precision warrants testing, but the label alone does not demonstrate a provider changed the original weights.</p> <p><strong>GPT-OSS provides a concrete example.</strong> OpenAI’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="gpt-oss-120b release documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://huggingface.co/openai/gpt-oss-120b/raw/main/README.md"> <a href="https://huggingface.co/openai/gpt-oss-120b/raw/main/README.md" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >gpt-oss-120b release documentation</a> </span> states its mixture-of-experts weights use MXFP4 and its evaluations used the same quantization. A four-bit label for those weights is consistent with the published release. It is not evidence of an additional provider downgrade.</p> <p><strong>Upcasting</strong> converts stored values into a wider representation. Converting an already quantized checkpoint to BF16 does not recover information discarded during quantization. Conversely, converting an originally higher-precision checkpoint to four bits introduces a separate change worth evaluating.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Observation</th> <th>Supported conclusion</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Native MXFP4 checkpoint</strong></td> <td>Four-bit expert weights belong to the release</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>BF16 endpoint label</strong></td> <td>A wider reported format, without proof of better answers</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Unknown precision</strong></td> <td>Missing metadata, without proof of hidden degradation</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Matching precision labels</strong></td> <td>Insufficient evidence of equivalent serving behavior</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Matching labels also fail to rule out quantization differences.</strong> They omit details such as which tensors were quantized, calibration choices, and execution kernels. Test the complete endpoint instead of treating bit depth as a quality ranking.</p> <h2 id="check-the-token-budget"> <a href="#check-the-token-budget" title="Check the Token Budget">Check the Token Budget</a> <a href="#check-the-token-budget" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Check the Token Budget">#</a> </h2> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>curl --fail --silent --show-error <span style="color:#ae81ff">\ </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#e6db74">'https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models/openai/gpt-oss-120b/endpoints'</span> <span style="color:#ae81ff">\ </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> | jq <span style="color:#e6db74">'.data.endpoints[] | { </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> name, </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> provider_name, </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> context_length, </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> max_completion_tokens, </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> supported_parameters, </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> quantization, </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> pricing </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> }'</span> </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>The endpoints API</strong> exposes provider-level metadata for one model. This command needs <strong><code>curl</code></strong> and <strong><code>jq</code></strong>. Inspect the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="live gpt-oss-120b endpoint response"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models/openai/gpt-oss-120b/endpoints"> <a href="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models/openai/gpt-oss-120b/endpoints" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >live gpt-oss-120b endpoint response</a> </span> before selecting a service. Treat missing or null fields as unknown rather than unlimited. Save a dated local snapshot when comparing results.</p> <p><strong>A check on October 5, 2026</strong> returned these advertised limits for gpt-oss-120b. These are metadata values, not measured completion lengths, and providers change them over time.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Provider</th> <th style="text-align: right">Context tokens</th> <th style="text-align: right">Maximum completion tokens</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>DigitalOcean</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">128,000</td> <td style="text-align: right">4,096</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Novita</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">131,072</td> <td style="text-align: right">32,768</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Together</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">131,072</td> <td style="text-align: right">117,964</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Context length and output length are separate limits.</strong> A long-context model still needs sufficient room for its answer. Conversation history, system instructions, and tool definitions consume space alongside the user’s document.</p> <p><strong>Reasoning tokens</strong> also consume generation budget on supported reasoning models. A small allowance risks incomplete reasoning, little visible output, or termination before a final answer. Inspect usage and the finish reason rather than assuming every short answer reflects weaker weights. OpenRouter explains this budgeting in its <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="reasoning-token documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/best-practices/reasoning-tokens"> <a href="https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/best-practices/reasoning-tokens" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >reasoning-token documentation</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>An explicit <code>max_tokens</code></strong> gives the router a requested output length to match against provider support. Choose it from measured task needs and available context. Setting an excessive value narrows eligibility and does not guarantee a longer or better answer.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/context-reasoning-output-token-budget.webp", "caption": "Illustration of a divided token pool flowing through a model into an output stream", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-10-07 21:49:43.48357175 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b546.449186459", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-10-07 21:49:43.48357175 +0000 UTC m=+546.449186459"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/context-reasoning-output-token-budget.webp" alt="Illustration of a divided token pool flowing through a model into an output stream"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> <figcaption align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemprop="caption description"> <p>Conceptual token allocation, with reasoning and visible output sharing the completion allowance on supported providers</p> </figcaption> </figure> </center> <h2 id="require-your-parameters"> <a href="#require-your-parameters" title="Require Your Parameters">Require Your Parameters</a> <a href="#require-your-parameters" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Require Your Parameters">#</a> </h2> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-json" data-lang="json"><span style="display:flex;"><span>{ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">"model"</span>: <span style="color:#e6db74">"openai/gpt-oss-120b"</span>, </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">"messages"</span>: [ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> {<span style="color:#f92672">"role"</span>: <span style="color:#e6db74">"user"</span>, <span style="color:#f92672">"content"</span>: <span style="color:#e6db74">"Explain the failure modes of a retry loop."</span>} </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> ], </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">"max_tokens"</span>: <span style="color:#ae81ff">8192</span>, </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">"provider"</span>: { </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">"require_parameters"</span>: <span style="color:#66d9ef">true</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> } </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>} </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong><code>require_parameters</code></strong> defaults to false. Under default routing, unsupported parameters do not necessarily exclude an endpoint. OpenRouter documents providers ignoring unknown parameters. Setting this field to true filters routing by declared support.</p> <p><strong>Support metadata is not a behavioral guarantee.</strong> An endpoint advertising seed support still needs reproducibility testing. A tool-capable endpoint still needs schema validation and application-level tests. The filter prevents known incompatibilities from entering the candidate set.</p> <h2 id="pin-providers-deliberately"> <a href="#pin-providers-deliberately" title="Pin Providers Deliberately">Pin Providers Deliberately</a> <a href="#pin-providers-deliberately" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Pin Providers Deliberately">#</a> </h2> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-json" data-lang="json"><span style="display:flex;"><span>{ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">"model"</span>: <span style="color:#e6db74">"openai/gpt-oss-120b"</span>, </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">"messages"</span>: [ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> {<span style="color:#f92672">"role"</span>: <span style="color:#e6db74">"user"</span>, <span style="color:#f92672">"content"</span>: <span style="color:#e6db74">"Summarize the supplied incident report."</span>} </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> ], </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">"max_tokens"</span>: <span style="color:#ae81ff">8192</span>, </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">"provider"</span>: { </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">"order"</span>: [<span style="color:#e6db74">"REPLACE_WITH_VERIFIED_PROVIDER_SLUG"</span>], </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">"allow_fallbacks"</span>: <span style="color:#66d9ef">false</span>, </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">"require_parameters"</span>: <span style="color:#66d9ef">true</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> } </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>} </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Replace the placeholder</strong> with a provider slug copied from the model’s provider listing. Supply the report in your real request. This template is for configuration review, not a runnable request until you replace its placeholder.</p> <p><strong><code>order</code></strong> establishes preference. By itself, it leaves fallback to other providers enabled. Pairing it with <strong><code>allow_fallbacks: false</code></strong> restricts routing to the listed providers. Expect a failed request when none satisfies the request or remains available.</p> <p><strong>Endpoint variants need attention.</strong> A base provider slug matches multiple variants under the documented matching rules. Use the specific variant slug when testing a particular service configuration. Recheck the provider reported for each response.</p> <p><strong><code>quantizations</code></strong> is an allowlist of named formats, not a numerical minimum. An array containing <strong><code>"fp8"</code></strong> selects matching FP8 endpoints. It does not automatically include BF16 or all formats with more bits. Compare the original checkpoint first, then apply this filter only when your evaluation supports the restriction.</p> <h2 id="keep-quality-routing-enabled"> <a href="#keep-quality-routing-enabled" title="Keep Quality Routing Enabled">Keep Quality Routing Enabled</a> <a href="#keep-quality-routing-enabled" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Keep Quality Routing Enabled">#</a> </h2> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-json" data-lang="json"><span style="display:flex;"><span>{ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">"model"</span>: <span style="color:#e6db74">"openai/gpt-oss-120b:exacto"</span>, </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">"messages"</span>: [ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> {<span style="color:#f92672">"role"</span>: <span style="color:#e6db74">"user"</span>, <span style="color:#f92672">"content"</span>: <span style="color:#e6db74">"Compare the two supplied incident reports."</span>} </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> ], </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">"max_tokens"</span>: <span style="color:#ae81ff">8192</span>, </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">"provider"</span>: { </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">"require_parameters"</span>: <span style="color:#66d9ef">true</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> } </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>} </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Auto Exacto</strong> uses throughput, tool-call telemetry, and benchmarks to deprioritize underperforming providers. OpenRouter’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="March 2026 announcement"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://openrouter.ai/blog/announcements/auto-exacto/"> <a href="https://openrouter.ai/blog/announcements/auto-exacto/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >March 2026 announcement</a> </span> reports GLM-5 tool-call errors falling by 88%, with rates moving from roughly 8% toward 1%. It reports gpt-oss-120b moving from 5.6% to 3.5%.</p> <p><strong>Those are vendor-reported rollout results</strong>, not a promise for your application. Tool-call validity measures JSON, names, and schemas. A syntactically valid call still needs the correct arguments and action for the user’s task.</p> <p><strong>Requests containing tools</strong> receive Auto Exacto by default where the model has sufficient provider coverage. For other requests, <strong><code>:exacto</code></strong> opts into quality routing. The current documentation therefore supports quality routing for summarization and chat as well as tool use.</p> <p><strong><code>sort: "price"</code></strong>, the <strong><code>:floor</code></strong> suffix, and an account-level default price sort opt out of Auto Exacto. Check application settings and account preferences together. Consult the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Auto Exacto documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/auto-exacto"> <a href="https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/auto-exacto" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Auto Exacto documentation</a> </span> before combining routing controls.</p> <h2 id="calculate-your-workload-cost"> <a href="#calculate-your-workload-cost" title="Calculate Your Workload Cost">Calculate Your Workload Cost</a> <a href="#calculate-your-workload-cost" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Calculate Your Workload Cost">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Input price alone</strong> is an incomplete comparison. Consider these illustrative rates, expressed in dollars per million tokens. They demonstrate the arithmetic and are not current provider quotes.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Illustrative endpoint</th> <th style="text-align: right">Input price</th> <th style="text-align: right">Output price</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>A</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">$0.03</td> <td style="text-align: right">$16.00</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>B</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">$0.42</td> <td style="text-align: right">$1.32</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Workload: 6 million input tokens + 1 million output tokens </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>A = 6 × $0.03 + 1 × $16.00 = $16.18 </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>B = 6 × $0.42 + 1 × $1.32 = $3.84 </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Per million combined input and output tokens: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>A = $16.18 / 7 = $2.31 </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>B = $3.84 / 7 = $0.55 </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Endpoint A costs about 4.2 times as much</strong> for this mixture despite its lower input price. The 533-to-1 output/input price ratio on A is a ratio between two rates, not the user’s total cost multiplier. Different input/output proportions change the comparison.</p> <p><strong>API pricing units differ from comparison tables.</strong> The endpoint API expresses token prices per token. Multiply by one million before comparing them with the rates above.</p> <p><strong>Prompt caching</strong> introduces another variable. Cached reads, cache writes, and uncached input require separate accounting under the provider’s billing rules. Repeated text does not guarantee a cache hit. Check the reported cached-token counts and costs using the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="prompt caching documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/best-practices/prompt-caching"> <a href="https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/best-practices/prompt-caching" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >prompt caching documentation</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Routing affects cache continuity.</strong> OpenRouter documents sticky routing for caching, while manual provider order takes precedence. Auto Exacto also reorders providers and sometimes disrupts a warm cache. Compare observed cache savings against quality and retry costs before changing either policy.</p> <p><strong>Cost per accepted result</strong> is the useful application metric: divide total spend, including retries and failed attempts, by results meeting your acceptance criteria. Include any applicable non-token charges separately. A low token rate does not compensate for repeatedly unsuccessful tasks.</p> <h2 id="diagnose-an-inconsistent-answer"> <a href="#diagnose-an-inconsistent-answer" title="Diagnose an Inconsistent Answer">Diagnose an Inconsistent Answer</a> <a href="#diagnose-an-inconsistent-answer" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Diagnose an Inconsistent Answer">#</a> </h2> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Symptom</th> <th>First check</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Short or unfinished response</strong></td> <td>Finish reason, output allowance, reasoning usage</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Missing document details</strong></td> <td>Submitted content, endpoint context limit, client truncation</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Malformed tool call</strong></td> <td>Advertised support, tool schema, parsing behavior</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Different sampling behavior</strong></td> <td>Requested parameters and declared support</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Unexpected expense</strong></td> <td>Output volume, cache reads, retries, provider changes</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>No eligible provider</strong></td> <td>Conflicting limits, allowlists, and fallback restrictions</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Preserve the generation ID</strong> returned with the response. OpenRouter’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="generation metadata API"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://openrouter.ai/docs/api/api-reference/generations/get-request-&-usage-metadata-for-a-generation"> <a href="https://openrouter.ai/docs/api/api-reference/generations/get-request-&-usage-metadata-for-a-generation" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >generation metadata API</a> </span> exposes provider identity, usage, cost, and finish information. A session ID groups related work, but it does not replace the generation ID for a single-request lookup.</p> <p><strong>Compare endpoints under matching conditions.</strong> Use the same prompt, tools, reasoning settings, and token budget. Repeat across several representative tasks. Separate incomplete responses, invalid tool calls, and wrong answers instead of combining them into one unexplained quality score.</p> <p><strong>Benchmark uncertainty matters.</strong> Epoch AI’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="benchmarking analysis"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://epoch.ai/gradient-updates/why-benchmarking-is-hard"> <a href="https://epoch.ai/gradient-updates/why-benchmarking-is-hard" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >benchmarking analysis</a> </span> describes variation from implementations, sampling, and agent scaffolds. One disappointing answer does not establish a persistent provider defect or identify its cause.</p> <h2 id="endpoint-routing-walkthrough"> <a href="#endpoint-routing-walkthrough" title="Endpoint Routing Walkthrough">Endpoint Routing Walkthrough</a> <a href="#endpoint-routing-walkthrough" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Endpoint Routing Walkthrough">#</a> </h2> <script> function loadLiteYouTubeScript() { if (document.querySelector('script[src^="/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js"]')) { console.log('Lite YouTube script is already loaded.'); return; } var scriptTag = document.createElement('script'); scriptTag.src = '/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js'; scriptTag.setAttribute('defer', ''); scriptTag.setAttribute('type', 'module'); scriptTag.setAttribute('fetchpriority', 'low'); document.body.appendChild(scriptTag); } document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { if (typeof yieldToMain === 'function') { yieldToMain(loadLiteYouTubeScript, "user-visible"); } else { loadLiteYouTubeScript(); } }); </script> <style scoped> .lite-youtube-fallback { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; flex-direction: column; gap: 1em; padding: 1em; background-color: #000; color: #fff; text-decoration: none; } .lite-youtube-fallback::before { display: block; content: ''; border: solid transparent; border-width: 2em 0 2em 3em; border-left-color: red; } .lite-youtube-fallback:hover::before { border-left-color: #fff; } .lite-youtube-fallback:focus { outline: 2px solid red; } </style><div itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/VideoObject http://schema.org/LearningResource" style="position: relative; padding-bottom: 56.25%; height: 0; overflow: hidden;"> <meta itemprop="name" content="OpenRouter endpoint routing, precision, and pricing"> <meta itemprop="description" content="YouTube Video"> <meta itemprop="thumbnailUrl" content="https://img.youtube.com/vi/ZsnFX5mEJ4s/maxresdefault.jpg"> <meta itemprop="contentUrl" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZsnFX5mEJ4s"> <meta itemprop="learningResourceType" content="Concept Overview"> <meta itemprop="educationalLevel" content="High school (US)"> <lite-youtube videoid="ZsnFX5mEJ4s" videotitle="OpenRouter endpoint routing, precision, and pricing" videoplay="" nocookie posterloading="lazy" loading="lazy" params=""> <noscript> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZsnFX5mEJ4s" class="lite-youtube-fallback" style="position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; height: 100%; border:0;" title="OpenRouter endpoint routing, precision, and pricing"> <span class="lyt-visually-hidden"></span> </a> </noscript> </lite-youtube> </div> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": ["VideoObject", "LearningResource"], "name": "OpenRouter endpoint routing, precision, and pricing", "description": "YouTube Video", "thumbnailUrl": ["https:\/\/img.youtube.com\/vi\/ZsnFX5mEJ4s\/maxresdefault.jpg"], "contentUrl": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZsnFX5mEJ4s", "learningResourceType": "Concept Overview", "educationalLevel": "High school (US)" } </script> <p><strong>Further viewing:</strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="OpenRouter endpoint quality and routing discussion"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZsnFX5mEJ4s"> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZsnFX5mEJ4s" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >OpenRouter endpoint quality and routing discussion</a> </span> . Recheck endpoint listings before applying specific prices, limits, or provider comparisons.</p> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <ol> <li><strong>Inspect one model’s endpoints</strong> and record the limits relevant to your workload.</li> <li><strong>Select a routing policy</strong> with explicit parameter requirements and fallback behavior.</li> <li><strong>Test representative tasks</strong> against candidate endpoints and quality routing.</li> <li><strong>Record accepted-result cost</strong> alongside latency, cache usage, and failure categories.</li> <li><strong>Recheck after changes</strong> to model versions, serving behavior, or provider prices.</li> </ol> <p><strong>For broader AI fundamentals</strong>, continue with <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Basic AI Concepts"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/secai-plus/basic-ai-concepts/"> <a href="/secai-plus/basic-ai-concepts/" rel="follow me" >Basic AI Concepts</a> </span> .
