item.title: 32GB VRAM for Qwen 27B: The Local AI Hardware Guide for October 2026
item.category: "Local AI" , "AI Hardware" , "GPU Benchmarking" , "Self-Hosted AI" , "Computer Hardware" , "AI Economics"
item.description: A practical October 2026 guide to running a Qwen 27B model with 32GB of usable accelerator memory. Compare single GPUs, two-card builds, unified memory, used data-center cards, rented compute, software support, and full-context limits.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>32GB on the product label does not mean 32GB available to a Qwen 27B workload.</strong> The operating system, runtime, KV cache, model format, driver stack, and card layout all change the result. A cheap card with enough capacity might still lose badly on prompt processing or setup time.</p> <p><em>For October 2026, compare usable memory and completed work per dollar, not the VRAM number by itself.</em></p> <p>This guide looks at the practical ways to run a Qwen 27B model at 6-bit quality with a serious context window. It separates published specifications from reported test results, because one person’s tokens-per-second result is not a universal property of a GPU.</p> <h2 id="why-32gb-is-the-target"> <a href="#why-32gb-is-the-target" title="Why 32GB Is the Target">Why 32GB Is the Target</a> <a href="#why-32gb-is-the-target" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Why 32GB Is the Target">#</a> </h2> <p>The memory requirement starts with the weights. A dense 27B model reads the full parameter set during generation. At 6-bit quantization, the weights occupy roughly <strong>20.5GB</strong> before runtime allocations and context memory enter the calculation.</p> <p>A 128K-token context adds another large allocation. The exact KV-cache size changes with the model architecture, cache precision, batch settings, and backend. A practical estimate near <strong>8GB</strong> puts the combined weight and cache requirement around <strong>28.5GB</strong> before the operating system and inference runtime take their share.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Configuration</th> <th>What it supports</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>24GB discrete GPU</strong></td> <td>4-bit weights with reduced context, or partial offload</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>32GB discrete GPU</strong></td> <td>6-bit weights with a useful 128K context target</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Two 16GB GPUs</strong></td> <td>A split model with less headroom for runtime overhead</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>64GB unified memory</strong></td> <td>Larger context and model options, subject to the GPU memory allocation limit</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>The 32GB target is a sizing point, not a guarantee.</strong> A model may load while leaving too little room for a long prompt, a larger batch, multimodal inputs, or a second process.</p> <h2 id="the-video-is-one-useful-field-reference"> <a href="#the-video-is-one-useful-field-reference" title="The Video Is One Useful Field Reference">The Video Is One Useful Field Reference</a> <a href="#the-video-is-one-useful-field-reference" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Video Is One Useful Field Reference">#</a> </h2> <p>The following video presents a hands-on comparison of the main ways to reach 32GB for local AI. It is useful as a field reference for reported prices, setup friction, and runtime results. This article makes a separate comparison using hardware specifications, model memory behavior, software support, and total ownership cost.</p> <script> function loadLiteYouTubeScript() { if (document.querySelector('script[src^="/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js"]')) { console.log('Lite YouTube script is already loaded.'); return; } var scriptTag = document.createElement('script'); scriptTag.src = '/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js'; scriptTag.setAttribute('defer', ''); scriptTag.setAttribute('type', 'module'); scriptTag.setAttribute('fetchpriority', 'low'); document.body.appendChild(scriptTag); } document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { if (typeof yieldToMain === 'function') { yieldToMain(loadLiteYouTubeScript, "user-visible"); } else { loadLiteYouTubeScript(); } }); </script> <style scoped> .lite-youtube-fallback { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; flex-direction: column; gap: 1em; padding: 1em; background-color: #000; color: #fff; text-decoration: none; } .lite-youtube-fallback::before { display: block; content: ''; border: solid transparent; border-width: 2em 0 2em 3em; border-left-color: red; } .lite-youtube-fallback:hover::before { border-left-color: #fff; } .lite-youtube-fallback:focus { outline: 2px solid red; } </style><div itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/VideoObject http://schema.org/LearningResource" style="position: relative; padding-bottom: 56.25%; height: 0; overflow: hidden;"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Every Ways to Get 32GB VRAM for Local AI at Full Context"> <meta itemprop="description" content="A field comparison of single-GPU, multi-GPU, unified-memory, used accelerator, and rental paths for 32GB local AI workloads."> <meta itemprop="thumbnailUrl" content="https://img.youtube.com/vi/uavLRbbfM94/maxresdefault.jpg"> <meta itemprop="contentUrl" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uavLRbbfM94"> <meta itemprop="learningResourceType" content="Concept Overview"> <meta itemprop="educationalLevel" content="High school (US)"> <lite-youtube videoid="uavLRbbfM94" videotitle="Every Ways to Get 32GB VRAM for Local AI at Full Context" videoplay="" nocookie posterloading="lazy" loading="lazy" params=""> <noscript> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uavLRbbfM94" class="lite-youtube-fallback" style="position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; height: 100%; border:0;" title="Every Ways to Get 32GB VRAM for Local AI at Full Context"> <span class="lyt-visually-hidden"></span> </a> </noscript> </lite-youtube> </div> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": ["VideoObject", "LearningResource"], "name": "Every Ways to Get 32GB VRAM for Local AI at Full Context", "description": "A field comparison of single-GPU, multi-GPU, unified-memory, used accelerator, and rental paths for 32GB local AI workloads.", "thumbnailUrl": ["https:\/\/img.youtube.com\/vi\/uavLRbbfM94\/maxresdefault.jpg"], "contentUrl": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uavLRbbfM94", "learningResourceType": "Concept Overview", "educationalLevel": "High school (US)" } </script> <h2 id="usable-memory-beats-box-memory"> <a href="#usable-memory-beats-box-memory" title="Usable Memory Beats Box Memory">Usable Memory Beats Box Memory</a> <a href="#usable-memory-beats-box-memory" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Usable Memory Beats Box Memory">#</a> </h2> <h3 id="apple-unified-memory"> <a href="#apple-unified-memory" title="Apple Unified Memory">Apple Unified Memory</a> <a href="#apple-unified-memory" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Apple Unified Memory">#</a> </h3> <p>Apple silicon uses a shared pool for the CPU and GPU. Apple lists 32GB unified-memory Mac mini configurations, but the full pool is not a dedicated graphics allocation. macOS, the application, and the inference runtime all need space.</p> <p>Some llama.cpp sessions report roughly <strong>22,906MB available</strong> on a 32GB system. This is about <strong>21.3GiB</strong>, leaving little room for a 6-bit 27B model plus a large KV cache. The exact ceiling depends on the operating system, model runner, memory pressure, and launch settings.</p> <p>Apple silicon remains attractive for quiet systems. llama.cpp treats Metal as a first-class backend, and Apple avoids the driver and power issues found in many used data-center cards. The tradeoff is lower throughput than a high-end discrete GPU and less predictable memory headroom.</p> <h3 id="two-16gb-cards"> <a href="#two-16gb-cards" title="Two 16GB Cards">Two 16GB Cards</a> <a href="#two-16gb-cards" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Two 16GB Cards">#</a> </h3> <p>Two 16GB cards provide 32GB of physical VRAM, but the model runtime still needs per-device buffers and communication space. One card might report 13.4GB in use while the other reports 14.4GB. The remaining capacity is not a clean 4GB reserve for context.</p> <p>The split method also matters. <strong>Layer splitting</strong> assigns different model layers to different cards. It expands capacity, but the cards take turns through the model. <strong>Tensor splitting</strong> places work from the same layer across both cards, which increases communication but lets both devices contribute more directly.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Split method</th> <th>Main benefit</th> <th>Main cost</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Layer split</strong></td> <td>Simple capacity expansion</td> <td>One card often waits while the other works</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Tensor split</strong></td> <td>Better parallel compute in some workloads</td> <td>More tuning and more interconnect traffic</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>CPU plus GPU offload</strong></td> <td>Fits models above total VRAM</td> <td>Large speed penalty once the CPU handles frequent layers</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>A two-card plan needs a tested backend before purchase.</strong> PCIe generation, slot spacing, power delivery, driver support, and the exact quantization all affect the result.</p> <h2 id="single-card-options"> <a href="#single-card-options" title="Single-Card Options">Single-Card Options</a> <a href="#single-card-options" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Single-Card Options">#</a> </h2> <h3 id="rtx-5090"> <a href="#rtx-5090" title="RTX 5090">RTX 5090</a> <a href="#rtx-5090" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="RTX 5090">#</a> </h3> <p>NVIDIA lists the RTX 5090 with <strong>32GB of GDDR7</strong> and <strong>1,792GB/s of memory bandwidth</strong>. It has broad CUDA support, mature tooling, and many tested front ends. The current CUDA GPU table lists the RTX 5090 at compute capability 12.0.</p> <p>The price is the problem. A new 5090 gives a clean path to 32GB, but the purchase cost competes with months of rented accelerator time. It also draws up to <strong>575W total graphics power</strong>, so the system needs a serious power supply and cooling plan.</p> <h3 id="radeon-ai-pro-r9700"> <a href="#radeon-ai-pro-r9700" title="Radeon AI PRO R9700">Radeon AI PRO R9700</a> <a href="#radeon-ai-pro-r9700" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Radeon AI PRO R9700">#</a> </h3> <p>The R9700 is a 32GB-class AMD option with high memory bandwidth and a lower entry price than the 5090 in many listings. Its value depends heavily on the runtime. A default llama.cpp path might produce a usable result, while a faster community backend could produce a much higher result on the same card.</p> <p>This is the clearest example of why a GPU comparison needs two speed columns. <strong>Decode speed</strong> measures generated tokens. <strong>Prefill speed</strong> measures how quickly the backend reads the prompt before the first generated token. A 50,000-token codebase exposes a weak prefill path even when decode speed looks acceptable.</p> <h3 id="intel-arc-pro-b70"> <a href="#intel-arc-pro-b70" title="Intel Arc Pro B70">Intel Arc Pro B70</a> <a href="#intel-arc-pro-b70" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Intel Arc Pro B70">#</a> </h3> <p>The Arc Pro B70 targets professional workloads with 32GB of memory. It is an interesting capacity-per-dollar option, but the software path needs more inspection than CUDA hardware. Standard GGUF support, patched builds, draft-token settings, and backend maturity all affect the result.</p> <p><strong>A lower purchase price does not compensate for hours spent finding a working build.</strong> For a tinkerer, this work is part of the project. For a workstation used every day, driver and application support carry a real value.</p> <h2 id="used-data-center-cards"> <a href="#used-data-center-cards" title="Used Data-Center Cards">Used Data-Center Cards</a> <a href="#used-data-center-cards" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Used Data-Center Cards">#</a> </h2> <h3 id="tesla-v100"> <a href="#tesla-v100" title="Tesla V100">Tesla V100</a> <a href="#tesla-v100" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Tesla V100">#</a> </h3> <p>Used 32GB Tesla V100 cards attract attention because the card price looks low. The full build costs more. A passive data-center card needs airflow, a suitable chassis or shroud, power adapters, and a host with enough PCIe space.</p> <p>The other issue is software age. The current CUDA GPU table focuses on newer architectures and does not list the V100 in its current architecture table. A V100 owner needs to check the exact CUDA release, driver branch, backend, and community fork before buying.</p> <p><strong>Budget for a working V100 system, not a bare card.</strong> A card listed near $680 might become a roughly $1,000 project after cooling, adapters, and the host platform. Used prices also rise when a popular local-AI workload sends buyers toward the same retired accelerator.</p> <h3 id="amd-instinct-mi50"> <a href="#amd-instinct-mi50" title="AMD Instinct MI50">AMD Instinct MI50</a> <a href="#amd-instinct-mi50" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="AMD Instinct MI50">#</a> </h3> <p>The MI50 offers an attractive used price per gigabyte, yet its current software support is a serious constraint. A card that needs an older ROCm stack or a community-maintained fork is not equivalent to a current consumer card with mainstream application support.</p> <p>The reported prompt-processing gap is more important than the sticker price. One comparison measured about <strong>128 tokens per second</strong> on an MI50 against roughly <strong>2,652 tokens per second</strong> on a newer 32GB card for a prompt-processing workload. A 50,000-token codebase would take minutes on the slower path and seconds on the faster path before generation begins.</p> <p><strong>MI50 fits a narrow use case.</strong> It suits a builder who values capacity above interaction speed and accepts driver maintenance. It is a poor choice for rapid codebase analysis when prefill time matters.</p> <h2 id="software-is-part-of-the-gpu"> <a href="#software-is-part-of-the-gpu" title="Software Is Part of the GPU">Software Is Part of the GPU</a> <a href="#software-is-part-of-the-gpu" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Software Is Part of the GPU">#</a> </h2> <p>llama.cpp supports CUDA, HIP, Metal, Vulkan, SYCL, and other backends. It also supports CPU plus GPU hybrid inference and multi-GPU use. Those features do not produce identical performance across vendors or model formats.</p> <p>The same physical card often shows large differences between:</p> <ul> <li><strong>A default application build</strong> with conservative settings.</li> <li><strong>A tuned llama.cpp build</strong> with backend-specific kernels.</li> <li><strong>A community fork</strong> with speculative or multi-token prediction.</li> <li><strong>A patched model format</strong> designed for one accelerator path.</li> </ul> <p>Reported results in the supplied comparison include roughly <strong>27 tokens per second</strong> for a default 32GB AMD path, about <strong>46 tokens per second</strong> with multi-token prediction, and much higher results on a specialized backend. The result is useful as evidence of software headroom. It is not a promise for a fresh installation.</p> <p><strong>Record the backend, commit, model file, quantization, context length, prompt length, batch size, and power state with every benchmark.</strong> Without those fields, tokens per second is an advertisement number.</p> <h2 id="renting-instead-of-buying"> <a href="#renting-instead-of-buying" title="Renting Instead of Buying">Renting Instead of Buying</a> <a href="#renting-instead-of-buying" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Renting Instead of Buying">#</a> </h2> <p>Renting a fast GPU changes the calculation. A reported RTX 5090 rental price near <strong>$0.69 per hour</strong> makes a $4,400 purchase equal to about <strong>6,377 rental hours</strong> before electricity, host hardware, maintenance, and resale value enter the comparison.</p> <p>That is close to nine months of continuous rental or about two years at eight hours per day. A two-card desktop purchase near $1,560 equals about 2,261 hours at the same rental rate. The rented 5090 also avoids local heat, noise, driver setup, and card failure.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Usage pattern</th> <th>Better first test</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>A few hours per week</strong></td> <td>Hosted model or rented GPU</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>A short project</strong></td> <td>Rent a 5090-class card and measure the real workload</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Daily interactive use</strong></td> <td>Buy only after testing the backend and context target</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Agents running overnight</strong></td> <td>Owned hardware becomes easier to justify</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Private data with steady load</strong></td> <td>Owned hardware with network isolation</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Rent before buying when the model, backend, or context length is still uncertain.</strong> One weekend of measured use is cheaper than a wrong workstation purchase.</p> <h2 id="buying-recommendations"> <a href="#buying-recommendations" title="Buying Recommendations">Buying Recommendations</a> <a href="#buying-recommendations" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Buying Recommendations">#</a> </h2> <h3 id="two-rtx-5060-ti-16gb-cards"> <a href="#two-rtx-5060-ti-16gb-cards" title="Two RTX 5060 Ti 16GB Cards">Two RTX 5060 Ti 16GB Cards</a> <a href="#two-rtx-5060-ti-16gb-cards" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Two RTX 5060 Ti 16GB Cards">#</a> </h3> <p>Two 16GB cards provide a practical CUDA path for buyers who need 32GB and want common tutorials, drivers, and front ends. Use tensor splitting only after verifying the model format and backend. Layer splitting is simpler, but it often leaves performance on the table.</p> <p>This route also needs a motherboard with two usable slots, enough power, and airflow between the cards. A pair of cards is not a small workstation build once the platform cost is included.</p> <h3 id="one-32gb-card"> <a href="#one-32gb-card" title="One 32GB Card">One 32GB Card</a> <a href="#one-32gb-card" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="One 32GB Card">#</a> </h3> <p>Choose a single 32GB card when reliability, warranty coverage, and simple deployment matter more than the lowest memory price. The R9700 and RTX 5090 represent different versions of this choice. The AMD path emphasizes capacity and price. The NVIDIA path emphasizes software breadth and mature CUDA support.</p> <h3 id="a-used-v100-or-mi50"> <a href="#a-used-v100-or-mi50" title="A Used V100 or MI50">A Used V100 or MI50</a> <a href="#a-used-v100-or-mi50" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="A Used V100 or MI50">#</a> </h3> <p>Choose used data-center hardware only when the project itself includes driver testing, cooling work, and backend maintenance. The card price is the first line of the budget, not the final line.</p> <h3 id="apple-silicon"> <a href="#apple-silicon" title="Apple Silicon">Apple Silicon</a> <a href="#apple-silicon" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Apple Silicon">#</a> </h3> <p>Choose a 32GB Apple silicon system when silence, low idle power, and a compact desktop matter more than maximum throughput. Check the memory allocation reported by the exact runner before assuming a full 32GB is available to the model.</p> <h3 id="cloud-rental"> <a href="#cloud-rental" title="Cloud Rental">Cloud Rental</a> <a href="#cloud-rental" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Cloud Rental">#</a> </h3> <p>Choose rental when the workload is occasional, the model changes often, or a fast prompt response matters more than local ownership. Shut the instance down after the test. Idle time removes the price advantage quickly.</p> <h2 id="a-better-comparison-worksheet"> <a href="#a-better-comparison-worksheet" title="A Better Comparison Worksheet">A Better Comparison Worksheet</a> <a href="#a-better-comparison-worksheet" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="A Better Comparison Worksheet">#</a> </h2> <p>Before buying, record these values for every candidate:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Usable model memory</strong> after runtime overhead.</li> <li><strong>Weight format</strong> and expected model size.</li> <li><strong>KV-cache size</strong> at the target context length.</li> <li><strong>Prefill speed</strong> for a representative prompt.</li> <li><strong>Decode speed</strong> after the context is full.</li> <li><strong>Backend and driver version</strong> required for the result.</li> <li><strong>Idle and loaded power</strong> at your local electricity rate.</li> <li><strong>Host cost</strong>, cooling, adapters, storage, and warranty.</li> <li><strong>Rental equivalent</strong> for the number of hours you expect to use the system.</li> </ul> <p>The most useful test is a prompt from your real workload. For coding, use a representative codebase. For research, use a long document with the normal retrieval or paste workflow. Measure time to first token, prompt processing time, generation speed, memory use, and output quality.</p> <h2 id="final-recommendation"> <a href="#final-recommendation" title="Final Recommendation">Final Recommendation</a> <a href="#final-recommendation" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Final Recommendation">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Buy two RTX 5060 Ti 16GB cards for the lowest-friction 32GB CUDA build.</strong> Use a tensor-split configuration only after a small test confirms the backend works as expected.</p> <p><strong>Buy a single 32GB card when you need a cleaner workstation.</strong> Prefer the card with the stronger software path for your chosen runner, not the card with the lowest dollars-per-gigabyte figure.</p> <p><strong>Use a V100 or MI50 only when you accept the maintenance project.</strong> A cheap accelerator with weak prefill performance is not a bargain for long codebase prompts.</p> <p><strong>Rent a 5090-class GPU when use is irregular.</strong> The rental test gives you real memory, speed, and context data before a large purchase.</p> <p>The 32GB question is therefore not “Which card has the cheapest gigabyte?” It is “Which system leaves enough usable memory, reads my workload quickly, works with my software, and earns its purchase price through regular use?”</p> <h2 id="references"> <a href="#references" title="References">References</a> <a href="#references" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="References">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta target="_blank" >NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 specifications</a> </span> , official VRAM, bandwidth, power, and CUDA capability details.</li> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> item.title: The 64GB DGX Spark Is a Warning Sign for Local AI Hardware Prices
item.description: NVIDIA's 64GB DGX Spark tier shows how memory supply pressure is shaping local AI hardware. This guide explains the capacity cut, unified-memory tradeoffs, and why DRAM relief is unlikely before late 2027.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>The 64GB DGX Spark is a market signal for local AI buyers.</strong> A lower-memory configuration is arriving while demand for AI servers, HBM, and conventional DRAM remains high. The change does not prove every component is identical to the 128GB system, but it shows how vendors are responding to memory cost, availability, and product segmentation.</p> <p><em>If you need a local AI system with large shared memory, waiting for a quick price collapse is a weak plan. Set a budget, track memory capacity per dollar, and keep a second hardware path ready.</em></p> <h2 id="what-changed"> <a href="#what-changed" title="What Changed?">What Changed?</a> <a href="#what-changed" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Changed?">#</a> </h2> <p>The reported 64GB DGX Spark adds a lower-capacity tier to NVIDIA’s compact Grace Blackwell system. Tom’s Hardware reports a $4,999 starting price for the 64GB unit and a $6,950 price for the 128GB model. The two tiers target different memory budgets while keeping the same general product family and GB10 platform. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Tom’s Hardware reports the product and pricing details"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/gpus/nvidia-introduces-64gb-dgx-spark-to-throw-local-ai-fans-a-lifeline-amid-the-rampocalypse-new-gb10-config-starts-at-usd4999-for-those-who-can-work-with-less"> <a href="https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/gpus/nvidia-introduces-64gb-dgx-spark-to-throw-local-ai-fans-a-lifeline-amid-the-rampocalypse-new-gb10-config-starts-at-usd4999-for-those-who-can-work-with-less" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Tom’s Hardware reports the product and pricing details</a> </span> .</p> <p>NVIDIA’s own documentation lists the standard DGX Spark configuration with <strong>128GB of LPDDR5x unified system memory</strong>, a 256-bit interface, and 273GB/s of bandwidth. The memory is shared by the CPU and GPU instead of being split into ordinary system RAM and a separate graphics card pool. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="NVIDIA’s DGX Spark hardware guide documents the memory design"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.nvidia.com/dgx/dgx-spark/hardware.html"> <a href="https://docs.nvidia.com/dgx/dgx-spark/hardware.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >NVIDIA’s DGX Spark hardware guide documents the memory design</a> </span> .</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Configuration</th> <th style="text-align: right">Shared memory</th> <th style="text-align: right">Listed price</th> <th>Best fit</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>DGX Spark 64GB</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">64GB</td> <td style="text-align: right">$4,999 reported starting price</td> <td>Smaller models, shorter context, and lower entry cost</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>DGX Spark 128GB</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">128GB</td> <td style="text-align: right">$6,950 reported price for the new tier</td> <td>Larger models, longer context, and more memory headroom</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>The 64GB model is not a free performance upgrade.</strong> It gives buyers a lower purchase price, but it also removes half of the shared memory pool. A model fitting in 128GB with room for weights, runtime overhead, KV cache, and a second process is not guaranteed to fit comfortably in 64GB.</p> <h2 id="why-capacity-matters"> <a href="#why-capacity-matters" title="Why Capacity Matters">Why Capacity Matters</a> <a href="#why-capacity-matters" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Why Capacity Matters">#</a> </h2> <p>Local AI systems need memory for more than model weights. The runtime also holds the KV cache, temporary tensors, tokenizer state, operating-system allocations, and application data. Long prompts and larger batches increase the cache requirement.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Workload factor</th> <th>Memory pressure</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Model weights</strong></td> <td>The quantized model file must fit with runtime overhead</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Context length</strong></td> <td>Longer prompts grow the KV cache</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Batch size</strong></td> <td>More simultaneous sequences need more working memory</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Quantization</strong></td> <td>Smaller formats reduce weight storage but change quality and speed tradeoffs</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Multiple services</strong></td> <td>Embeddings, reranking, databases, and the model share the same machine</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>A 64GB system suits a narrower workload envelope.</strong> It remains useful for smaller local models and focused inference. It is a weaker choice for a buyer who expects to move from an 8B model to a 27B, 70B, or multimodal model without replacing the system.</p> <p>The 128GB system also gives you more room for model experimentation. Local model formats, context settings, and serving tools change faster than a small workstation’s replacement cycle.</p> <h2 id="this-is-a-supply-signal"> <a href="#this-is-a-supply-signal" title="This Is a Supply Signal">This Is a Supply Signal</a> <a href="#this-is-a-supply-signal" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="This Is a Supply Signal">#</a> </h2> <p>The capacity change matters because it arrives during a memory squeeze. A vendor offering less memory at a lower tier suggests an attempt to serve buyers who cannot justify the larger price, while preserving a premium tier for buyers who need the full capacity.</p> <p>This is an interpretation, not proof of NVIDIA’s internal supply decisions. The public product information does not establish whether the 64GB unit uses the same memory package, the same board configuration, or a different allocation path. The visible signal is simpler: memory capacity is becoming a product-level pricing lever.</p> <p><strong>Capacity cuts do not automatically produce cheap hardware.</strong> A 64GB model at $4,999 still asks local AI buyers to spend workstation money for a system with less shared memory than the original configuration. Buyers should compare usable memory, bandwidth, software support, storage, and warranty terms instead of comparing the sticker price alone.</p> <h2 id="why-dram-relief-is-delayed"> <a href="#why-dram-relief-is-delayed" title="Why DRAM Relief Is Delayed">Why DRAM Relief Is Delayed</a> <a href="#why-dram-relief-is-delayed" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Why DRAM Relief Is Delayed">#</a> </h2> <p>TrendForce’s July 30, 2026 outlook says DRAM supply should remain constrained through 2027. The firm points to HBM allocation, AI server demand, CPU memory procurement, and the long schedule for new production capacity. It expects meaningful output from new capacity to arrive mainly in the second half of 2027, with substantial contributions delayed into 2028. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Read TrendForce’s DRAM and NAND outlook"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.trendforce.com/presscenter/news/20260730-13158.html"> <a href="https://www.trendforce.com/presscenter/news/20260730-13158.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Read TrendForce’s DRAM and NAND outlook</a> </span> .</p> <p>TrendForce’s September 29, 2026 HBM outlook is even less favorable for a fast reset. It says HBM and conventional DRAM continue competing for advanced-process and wafer capacity, with the HBM market expected to remain supply constrained in 2027. The report also says some accelerator vendors are evaluating lower-stack HBM configurations to manage supply and cost. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Read the September HBM outlook"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.trendforce.com/presscenter/news/20260929-13255.html"> <a href="https://www.trendforce.com/presscenter/news/20260929-13255.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Read the September HBM outlook</a> </span> .</p> <p>The production cycle explains the timing. A new fab needs construction, equipment installation, qualification, process migration, and yield improvement. A public announcement does not create finished memory modules on retail shelves. Even after wafer output rises, suppliers first serve contracted server and accelerator demand.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Time window</th> <th>What to expect</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Now through 2026</strong></td> <td>High AI demand keeps memory allocation tight and prices unstable</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>First half of 2027</strong></td> <td>New capacity exists in planning and construction, but broad retail relief remains uncertain</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Second half of 2027</strong></td> <td>Some new output is due, with regional and product-specific differences</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>2028</strong></td> <td>A stronger chance for meaningful supply growth, assuming demand does not accelerate again</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em><strong>Late 2027 is a relief window, not a promise of cheap RAM.</strong></em> Continued demand growth, HBM allocation, tariffs, currency movement, and supplier contracts leave broad retail relief exposed to a 2028 delay.</p> <h2 id="dram-is-not-nand"> <a href="#dram-is-not-nand" title="DRAM Is Not NAND">DRAM Is Not NAND</a> <a href="#dram-is-not-nand" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="DRAM Is Not NAND">#</a> </h2> <p>The memory crisis affects product categories differently. TrendForce expects NAND Flash conditions to loosen during the second half of 2027 as new capacity and process migration raise output while consumer electronics demand stays weak. DRAM faces a tighter path because HBM and server memory consume scarce wafer capacity.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Memory type</th> <th>Main local AI role</th> <th>2027 outlook</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>DRAM</strong></td> <td>System memory, GPU memory, and server modules</td> <td>Supply remains tight, with relief more likely late in 2027 or later</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>HBM</strong></td> <td>High-bandwidth memory beside AI accelerators</td> <td>Supply remains constrained and pricing pressure stays high</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>NAND Flash</strong></td> <td>SSD storage for models and datasets</td> <td>Supply conditions have a better chance of easing sooner, especially in the second half of 2027</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>A cheaper SSD does not solve a VRAM or unified-memory shortage.</strong> Local AI buyers often need more model memory first. Storage prices matter after the model fits in the available memory pool.</p> <h2 id="what-this-means-for-local-ai-buyers"> <a href="#what-this-means-for-local-ai-buyers" title="What This Means for Local AI Buyers">What This Means for Local AI Buyers</a> <a href="#what-this-means-for-local-ai-buyers" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What This Means for Local AI Buyers">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Buy for the model you expect to run, not the model you use this week.</strong> An 8B model often works well in 64GB, while a 27B or 70B model needs more space or more aggressive quantization. A memory limit also affects context length, concurrent requests, and the ability to run support services beside the model.</p> <ul> <li><strong>Choose 64GB</strong> when your workload stays within smaller models and a single active service.</li> <li><strong>Choose 128GB</strong> when you need long context, larger models, multimodal experiments, or room for future model changes.</li> <li><strong>Choose a discrete GPU workstation</strong> when you need replaceable graphics hardware, more VRAM options, or broader software support.</li> <li><strong>Choose rented compute</strong> when your workload is occasional and the purchase price would leave the system idle.</li> <li><strong>Choose a used system</strong> only after checking memory health, warranty coverage, power use, driver support, and the real price per usable gigabyte.</li> </ul> <p>The 64GB DGX Spark also changes the comparison set. A buyer should compare it with a 128GB DGX Spark, a 96GB or 128GB professional GPU workstation, a used 48GB or 80GB accelerator, and short-term cloud rentals. The right answer depends on model size, context length, uptime, privacy needs, and repair expectations.</p> <h2 id="a-practical-buying-method"> <a href="#a-practical-buying-method" title="A Practical Buying Method">A Practical Buying Method</a> <a href="#a-practical-buying-method" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="A Practical Buying Method">#</a> </h2> <p>Use a simple worksheet before spending money:</p> <ol> <li><strong>List the models.</strong> Record the quantized file size, expected runtime overhead, and target context length.</li> <li><strong>Add memory headroom.</strong> Leave room for KV cache, the operating system, storage services, and monitoring.</li> <li><strong>Record the actual price.</strong> Include storage, shipping, tax, warranty, and power equipment.</li> <li><strong>Calculate usable capacity per dollar.</strong> Do not use advertised capacity alone if the runtime reserves part of the pool.</li> <li><strong>Test before buying.</strong> Rent comparable hardware and measure load time, decode speed, prompt length, and stability.</li> <li><strong>Set a replacement trigger.</strong> Decide whether a future model or context target would force an upgrade.</li> </ol> <p><strong>Do not pay a premium for capacity you will never use.</strong> <strong>Do not buy a low-capacity system for a model exceeding its practical memory limit.</strong> Both mistakes turn a memory shortage into an avoidable hardware replacement.</p> <h2 id="the-bottom-line"> <a href="#the-bottom-line" title="The Bottom Line">The Bottom Line</a> <a href="#the-bottom-line" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Bottom Line">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>The 64GB DGX Spark is useful as a lower entry tier, but it is also a warning about local AI hardware economics.</strong> Memory is now a primary product constraint. A vendor creates a lower price point by reducing capacity, while the high-memory tier remains expensive because the underlying supply problem persists.</p> <p>The market evidence does not support planning around an immediate DDR5 or DRAM price collapse. TrendForce expects tight DRAM and HBM conditions through 2027, with new capacity ramping late in the year and stronger output arriving later. NAND has a better chance of easing sooner, but cheaper SSDs do not replace more model memory.</p> <p>For a buyer in October 2026, the practical choices are clear. Buy 64GB for a bounded workload, pay for 128GB when model flexibility matters, rent during uncertain demand, or wait with a specific price target and a backup plan. Waiting without a target leaves you exposed to another product refresh, another allocation shift, or another year of high memory costs.</p> <h2 id="references"> <a href="#references" item.title: How to Disable Contactless Payment on a Credit Card
item.description: A practical guide to disabling contactless payment on a spare credit card while keeping chip and magnetic-stripe payments available, with safety limits and better alternatives.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>A contactless card has a separate NFC antenna.</strong> If you keep the card inside a phone case, the antenna triggers card clash or repeated NFC alerts on some phones. A physical break in the antenna loop disables tap to pay while the chip and magnetic stripe remain available on some cards.</p> <p><em>Use a spare card for this project. Treat the modification as permanent, and confirm the result with the card issuer before relying on it.</em></p> <h2 id="why-disable-contactless-payment"> <a href="#why-disable-contactless-payment" title="Why Disable Contactless Payment?">Why Disable Contactless Payment?</a> <a href="#why-disable-contactless-payment" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Why Disable Contactless Payment?">#</a> </h2> <p>Tap to pay is convenient, and modern mobile wallets add another payment token to the same phone. The problem starts when an NFC-enabled physical card sits close to the phone’s NFC reader.</p> <p>Two payment instruments might answer the same reader. Android might also detect the physical card when you open or handle the phone. Removing the card from the case solves the problem, but it adds friction every time you pay.</p> <p>The goal here is narrow: disable the card’s contactless interface while keeping other payment methods available.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Payment method</th> <th>Expected result after an antenna break</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Contactless payment</strong></td> <td>Disabled because the NFC antenna loop no longer couples with a reader</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>EMV chip</strong></td> <td>Often remains available if the chip and its contacts are untouched</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Magnetic stripe</strong></td> <td>Often remains available if the stripe is untouched</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Online card payments</strong></td> <td>Usually unaffected, but the issuer might replace or deactivate the card after damage</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="how-the-card-works"> <a href="#how-the-card-works" title="How the Card Works">How the Card Works</a> <a href="#how-the-card-works" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="How the Card Works">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>The NFC antenna is a thin conductive loop inside the plastic.</strong> It usually runs around much of the card perimeter. A contactless reader powers the card through this loop and exchanges data with the embedded NFC chip.</p> <p>The EMV contact chip uses exposed metal contacts on the card face. The magnetic stripe uses a separate strip along the back. These systems share the same card body, but they do not need the same antenna loop.</p> <p>This separation explains the modification. Breaking the loop stops NFC communication. It does not erase the card number, destroy the stripe, or remove the EMV contacts when the cut stays clear of those components.</p> <h2 id="the-lower-risk-options"> <a href="#the-lower-risk-options" title="The Lower-Risk Options">The Lower-Risk Options</a> <a href="#the-lower-risk-options" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Lower-Risk Options">#</a> </h2> <p>Physical modification is a last resort. Check these options first:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Ask the issuer for a non-contactless replacement.</strong> Some issuers offer card variants without tap to pay.</li> <li><strong>Store the card away from the phone.</strong> A separate sleeve removes the NFC collision without changing the card.</li> <li><strong>Use a card holder with shielding.</strong> Test the holder with the phone and the card before depending on it for payment.</li> <li><strong>Use a virtual wallet token.</strong> Apple Pay and Google Pay let the phone handle contactless payment while the physical card stays in reserve.</li> <li><strong>Use a different backup card.</strong> Keeping the modified card out of daily service avoids a failure at a merchant.</li> </ul> <p><em>Do not microwave, burn, bend, or puncture the card near the chip. Those methods create unnecessary damage and might expose you to heat, sharp fragments, or a failed backup payment method.</em></p> <h2 id="antenna-modification"> <a href="#antenna-modification" title="Antenna Modification">Antenna Modification</a> <a href="#antenna-modification" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Antenna Modification">#</a> </h2> <p>The method described by the linked examples is simple in concept: locate the antenna loop, then make one small break in the loop with a fine tool. The exact antenna route differs by card design, so do not copy a location from one card to another.</p> <p>A bright flashlight behind the card might reveal the antenna path. Some cards show a visible wire or loop near the perimeter. Keep the break away from the EMV chip, its contacts, the magnetic stripe, embossed numbers, and any visible issuer markings.</p> <p>Work on a stable surface with eye protection. Secure the card before cutting or drilling. Use controlled pressure, stop when the loop is broken, and inspect both sides for cracks. A tiny cut or hole is enough. More damage does not improve the result.</p> <p>The result is permanent. A damaged card falls outside some issuer replacement policies, and a merchant terminal refuses cards with cracked bodies or misaligned contacts. Keep another payment method available before testing it.</p> <h2 id="test-the-result"> <a href="#test-the-result" title="Test the Result">Test the Result</a> <a href="#test-the-result" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Test the Result">#</a> </h2> <p>Test each function separately:</p> <ol> <li>Hold the card away from the phone and try it at a contactless reader. The tap should fail if the antenna loop is broken.</li> <li>Insert the card into a compatible terminal and test the EMV chip with the required PIN.</li> <li>Test the magnetic stripe only where the merchant and issuer still support it.</li> <li>Check the card account or call the issuer to confirm the card remains active.</li> <li>Add the card to the phone wallet only if the issuer supports the wallet token and you still want phone-based contactless payments.</li> </ol> <p>Do not test with an important purchase. Use a low-value transaction, and keep a second card or cash available.</p> <h2 id="video-demonstration"> <a href="#video-demonstration" title="Video Demonstration">Video Demonstration</a> <a href="#video-demonstration" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Video Demonstration">#</a> </h2> <p>The following video shows the physical modification and explains why breaking the antenna loop stops contactless operation:</p> <script> function loadLiteYouTubeScript() { if (document.querySelector('script[src^="/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js"]')) { console.log('Lite YouTube script is already loaded.'); return; } var scriptTag = document.createElement('script'); scriptTag.src = '/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js'; scriptTag.setAttribute('defer', ''); scriptTag.setAttribute('type', 'module'); scriptTag.setAttribute('fetchpriority', 'low'); document.body.appendChild(scriptTag); } document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { if (typeof yieldToMain === 'function') { yieldToMain(loadLiteYouTubeScript, "user-visible"); } else { loadLiteYouTubeScript(); } }); </script> <style scoped> .lite-youtube-fallback { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; flex-direction: column; gap: 1em; padding: 1em; background-color: #000; color: #fff; text-decoration: none; } .lite-youtube-fallback::before { display: block; content: ''; border: solid transparent; border-width: 2em 0 2em 3em; border-left-color: red; } .lite-youtube-fallback:hover::before { border-left-color: #fff; } .lite-youtube-fallback:focus { outline: 2px solid red; } </style><div itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/VideoObject http://schema.org/LearningResource" style="position: relative; padding-bottom: 56.25%; height: 0; overflow: hidden;"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Why Does My Credit Card Have a Hole in It?"> <meta itemprop="description" content="YouTube Video"> <meta itemprop="thumbnailUrl" content="https://img.youtube.com/vi/XH_st471JEU/maxresdefault.jpg"> <meta itemprop="contentUrl" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XH_st471JEU"> <meta itemprop="learningResourceType" content="Concept Overview"> <meta itemprop="educationalLevel" content="High school (US)"> <lite-youtube videoid="XH_st471JEU" videotitle="Why Does My Credit Card Have a Hole in It?" videoplay="" nocookie posterloading="lazy" loading="lazy" params=""> <noscript> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XH_st471JEU" class="lite-youtube-fallback" style="position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; height: 100%; border:0;" title="Why Does My Credit Card Have a Hole in It?"> <span class="lyt-visually-hidden"></span> </a> </noscript> </lite-youtube> </div> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": ["VideoObject", "LearningResource"], "name": "Why Does My Credit Card Have a Hole in It?", "description": "YouTube Video", "thumbnailUrl": ["https:\/\/img.youtube.com\/vi\/XH_st471JEU\/maxresdefault.jpg"], "contentUrl": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XH_st471JEU", "learningResourceType": "Concept Overview", "educationalLevel": "High school (US)" } </script> <p>The video is a demonstration, not a guarantee for every card design. Use it to understand the concept, then inspect your own card before deciding whether the risk is acceptable.</p> <h2 id="what-the-sources-show"> <a href="#what-the-sources-show" title="What the Sources Show">What the Sources Show</a> <a href="#what-the-sources-show" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What the Sources Show">#</a> </h2> <p>The examples below use two related approaches. Art Chaidarun describes making a small cut in the antenna loop while keeping the chip and stripe functional. The Instructables guide documents a similar physical approach for disabling contactless payment on a debit card. The forum discussion adds a useful warning: break the loop away from the EMV chip rather than drilling beside it.</p> <p>These reports describe individual cards. They do not establish a universal antenna layout or promise issuer approval after modification. Your card issuer’s replacement and deactivation rules control the final outcome.</p> <h2 id="references"> <a href="#references" title="References">References</a> <a href="#references" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="References">#</a> </h2> <ol> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Art Chaidarun, How to Disable Contactless Payment on a Credit Card"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://chaidarun.com/disable-contactless-payment"> <a href="https://chaidarun.com/disable-contactless-payment" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Art Chaidarun, How to Disable Contactless Payment on a Credit Card</a> </span> </li> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Instructables, How to Disable Contactless Payment on Your Debit Card"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.instructables.com/How-to-Disable-Contactless-Payment-on-Your-Debit-C/"> <a href="https://www.instructables.com/How-to-Disable-Contactless-Payment-on-Your-Debit-C/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Instructables, How to Disable Contactless Payment on Your Debit Card</a> </span> </li> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Dangerous Things Forum, Easiest way of disabling NFC in a credit card"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://forum.dangerousthings.com/t/easiest-way-of-disabling-nfc-in-a-credit-card/"> <a href="https://forum.dangerousthings.com/t/easiest-way-of-disabling-nfc-in-a-credit-card/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Dangerous Things Forum, Easiest way of disabling NFC in a credit card</a> </span> </li> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="DeviantOllam, Why Does My Credit Card Have a Hole in It?"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XH_st471JEU"> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XH_st471JEU" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >DeviantOllam, Why Does My Credit Card Have a Hole in It?</a> </span> </li> </ol> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p>If you need a payment card for a phone case, start with an issuer-approved non-contactless card or a separate sleeve. If you modify a spare card, test every remaining payment method before carrying it as your only backup.</p> <p>For related payment-card details, read the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Privacy.com virtual cards guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/privacy-com-virtual-debit-cards-security-privacy/"> <a href="/articles/privacy-com-virtual-debit-cards-security-privacy/" rel="follow me" >Privacy.com virtual cards guide</a> </span> and use the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="magnetic stripe decoder"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/magnetic-stripe-decoder/"> <a href="/magnetic-stripe-decoder/" rel="follow me" >magnetic stripe decoder</a> </span> to study the data stored on Tracks 1 and 2.</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Llama 3.1 8B and Qwen3.8 27B GPU Benchmarks on Vast.ai
item.category: "Local AI" , "GPU Benchmarking" , "Self-Hosted AI" , "Cloud Computing" , "Artificial Intelligence" , "AI Economics"
item.description: Measured Ollama benchmarks of Llama 3.1 8B and Qwen3.8 27B across leading Vast.ai GPUs. Compare decode speed, long-context behavior, rental cost, self-hosting tradeoffs, API credits, and subscriptions.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>The H100 SXM was the fastest card in both Ollama model tests, but it was not the best value.</strong> The RTX PRO 5000 and RTX 6000 Ada delivered a stronger speed-to-rental-cost balance, while the CMP 170HX offered the lowest hourly rate among the completed Qwen3.8 27B runs.</p> <p><em>These results measure one model, one Ollama wrapper, one default quantization, and one serving pattern. Treat them as sizing data for this workload, not as a universal GPU ranking.</em></p> <p>This article compares <strong>Llama 3.1:8b</strong>, an Ollama Q4_K_M build at 8.03B parameters, with <strong>Qwen3.8:27b</strong>, an Ollama Q4_K_M build at roughly 27.3B parameters. Both were tested across GPU instances rented from Vast.ai. The tests focused on decode throughput at actual prompt lengths up to the supported context limit.</p> <h2 id="the-short-answer"> <a href="#the-short-answer" title="The Short Answer">The Short Answer</a> <a href="#the-short-answer" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Short Answer">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Rent an RTX PRO 5000 or RTX 6000 Ada for regular single-user work.</strong> The RTX PRO 5000 led the value comparison at short and medium context lengths. The RTX 6000 Ada cost less and kept a useful lead over the A100 cards. Rent an H100 SXM when response speed matters more than hourly cost or when long prompts are part of the workload.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Goal</th> <th>Recommendation</th> <th>Reason</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Lowest test cost</strong></td> <td>CMP 170HX</td> <td>$0.420 per hour and enough VRAM for the tested Q4_K_M models</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Best value under $1.25/hr</strong></td> <td>RTX PRO 5000 or RTX 6000 Ada</td> <td>Strong decode speed without H100 rental cost</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Fastest replies</strong></td> <td>H100 SXM</td> <td>Highest decode speed in both model tests</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Long-context Qwen work</strong></td> <td>H100 SXM or RTX PRO 6000 Max-Q</td> <td>Both completed the approximately 131k-token Qwen run with substantial VRAM headroom</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Popular 8B baseline</strong></td> <td>Llama 3.1:8b</td> <td>A practical 8B comparison with a 128K context limit</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Small recurring workload</strong></td> <td>API credits or a chat subscription</td> <td>No idle GPU charge, maintenance, or deployment work</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Private and frequent workload</strong></td> <td>Owned GPU workstation</td> <td>Hardware cost becomes easier to justify with sustained utilization</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Abliterated or uncensored experiments</strong></td> <td>Rent first, then buy only after sustained use</td> <td>Model behavior, licensing, and operational risk deserve a separate test before hardware spend</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="what-was-tested"> <a href="#what-was-tested" title="What Was Tested">What Was Tested</a> <a href="#what-was-tested" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Was Tested">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>The benchmark used Ollama with the default Q4_K_M model build.</strong> No special quantization, speculative decoding, custom sampler, or serving stack was added. The goal was a simple, locally reproducible comparison of the GPU instances.</p> <p>Vast.ai describes its service as a GPU cloud marketplace connecting compute providers with users. Its documentation lists on-demand, reserved, interruptible, and serverless options, with search filters for GPU model, memory, price, and availability. The hourly rates below came from the selected instances during this benchmark session, not from a permanent Vast.ai price list.</p> <p>The measured output was <strong>decode throughput</strong>, expressed as generated tokens per second. Prefill throughput is listed separately because it describes prompt processing, not the speed at which the answer appears. A long prompt often takes substantial time to process even when decode speed remains high.</p> <p>The benchmark used two valid trials per context and recorded the median decode result. The completed prompt levels were based on actual <code>prompt_eval_count</code> values:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Approximately 16.4k prompt tokens</strong></li> <li><strong>Approximately 32.8k prompt tokens</strong></li> <li><strong>Approximately 65.5k prompt tokens</strong></li> <li><strong>Approximately 131k prompt tokens</strong></li> </ul> <p>The requested 256k-token run was not completed. The 40 GB A100 cards and several smaller cards were still processing or failed to finish at the target context length.</p> <blockquote> <p><strong>Benchmark limit:</strong> The figures describe two Ollama Q4_K_M workloads under one serving pattern. They do not predict training speed, multi-user throughput, image generation speed, vLLM performance, or another model’s result.</p> </blockquote> <h2 id="llama-31-8b-rerun"> <a href="#llama-31-8b-rerun" title="Llama 3.1 8B Rerun">Llama 3.1 8B Rerun</a> <a href="#llama-31-8b-rerun" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Llama 3.1 8B Rerun">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Llama 3.1:8b provides a useful practical baseline for the same GPU pool.</strong> Ollama lists the model at roughly 120 million downloads, which makes it a reasonable popularity-based choice for a second benchmark. The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="official Ollama model page"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://ollama.com/library/llama3.1:8b"> <a href="https://ollama.com/library/llama3.1:8b" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >official Ollama model page</a> </span> lists a 4.9 GB Q4_K_M build, 8.03B parameters, and a 128K context window.</p> <p>The rerun used a model-specific benchmark runner and calibrated the prompt generator against Ollama’s tokenizer. The labels below use actual prompt counts rather than requested context settings:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Approximately 32,676 actual prompt tokens</strong> for the 32k target</li> <li><strong>Approximately 65,342 actual prompt tokens</strong> for the 64k target</li> <li><strong>Approximately 130,671 actual prompt tokens</strong> for the 128k target</li> </ul> <p>The 256k level is explicitly unsupported for Llama 3.1 8B because the model’s listed context limit is 128K. The runner added retry handling and status rows, so a timeout remains visible instead of disappearing from the table.</p> <h3 id="llama-31-8b-results"> <a href="#llama-31-8b-results" title="Llama 3.1 8B Results">Llama 3.1 8B Results</a> <a href="#llama-31-8b-results" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Llama 3.1 8B Results">#</a> </h3> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>GPU</th> <th SXM</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right"><strong>163.5</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right"><strong>124.0</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right"><strong>82.4</strong></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>H100 SXM</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right"><strong>158.6</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right"><strong>121.2</strong></td> <td style="text-align: <td><strong>RTX 6000 Ada</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">88.3</td> <td style="text-align: right">53.9</td> <td style="text-align: right">29.3</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>RTX PRO 6000 style="text-align: right">20.3</td> <td style="text-align: right">20.3</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>2x RTX 5060 Ti</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">1.3</td> <td style="text-align: right">26.8</td> <td style="text-align: right">Timeout</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The two H100 rows came from separate valid instances of the same GPU class. Both were clearly ahead of the other cards. Their 32k results were 44% to 48% faster than the RTX PRO 5000, and their 128k results were about 61% to 65% faster.</p> <p>The A100 and RTX 5060 Ti 32k results are too low to represent comparable GPU execution for this workload. The RTX 5060 Ti host also timed out during the second 128k trial. Treat the host as unsuitable for valid GPU throughput comparisons rather than as a genuine ranking result.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Context target</th> <th>Status</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>32k</strong></td> <td>Completed on all 10 hosts</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>64k</strong></td> <td>Completed on all 10 hosts</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>128k</strong></td> <td>Completed on 9 hosts. The 2x RTX 5060 Ti host timed out during its second trial</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>256k</strong></td> <td>Unsupported for all hosts because Llama 3.1 8B supports up to 128K context</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="comparing-the-two-models"> <a href="#comparing-the-two-models" title="Comparing the Two Models">Comparing the Two Models</a> <a href="#comparing-the-two-models" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Comparing the Two Models">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>The smaller Llama model was faster on every comparable GPU, but model size and quality are not interchangeable.</strong> Llama 3.1 8B is useful for a popular, lower-memory baseline. Qwen3.8 27B needs more memory and delivers a different capability profile, so the numbers should guide hardware selection rather than declare one model universally better.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Use case</th> <th>Better benchmark reference</th> <th>Why</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Fast 8B assistant</strong></td> <td>Llama 3.1:8b</td> <td>Higher decode speed and lower model memory demand</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>27B local model sizing</strong></td> <td>Qwen3.8:27b</td> <td>More representative of a larger single-GPU workload</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>128K context ceiling</strong></td> <td>Llama 3.1:8b</td> <td>The model has an explicit 128K limit, so 256k is not a valid target</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Testing VRAM headroom</strong></td> <td>Qwen3.8:27b</td> <td>The larger model exposes memory and long-context limits sooner</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Cross-provider baseline</strong></td> <td>Llama 3.1:8b</td> <td>Popularity and model size make the result easier to reproduce</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The earlier Qwen rerun also corrected its actual prompt counts to approximately <strong>32,770</strong>, <strong>65,538</strong>, and <strong>131,074</strong> tokens on the supported context levels. Those corrected labels replace requested <code>num_ctx</code> values when comparing Qwen runs.</p> <h2 id="approximately-16k-tokens"> <a href="#approximately-16k-tokens" title="Approximately 16k right"><strong>39.4</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">124,653</td> <td style="text-align: right">$1.756/hr</td> </tr> <tr> <td style="text-align: right">5</td> <td><strong>RTX PRO 6000 Max-Q became the practical alternative to the H100 for long prompts. It delivered 67.8% of the H100’s decode speed at 56.0% of the hourly rate. The RTX 6000 Ada cost less, but its 48 GB of VRAM leaves less room for long prompts, larger batches, or another model configuration.</p> <h2 id="overall-decode-comparison"> <a href="#overall-decode-comparison" title="Overall Decode Comparison">Overall Decode Comparison</a> <a href="#overall-decode-comparison" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Overall Decode Comparison">#</a> </h2> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>GPU</th> <th style="text-align: right">~16k</th> <th style="text-align: right">~32.8k</th> <th style="text-align: right">~65.5k</th> <th right"><strong>120.0</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right"><strong>112.0</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right"><strong>108.2</strong></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>RTX PRO 5000</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">113.9</td> <td style="text-align: right">105.0</td> <td style="text-align: right">96.9</td> <td style="text-align: right">N/A</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>RTX 6000 Ada</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">89.1</td> <td style="text-align: right">75.7</td> <td style="text-align: right">70.8</td> <td style="text-align: right">61.7</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>RTX PRO 6000 Max-Q</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">84.1</td> <td style="text-align: right">66.9</td> <td style="text-align: right">75.7</td> <td style="text-align: right">73.4</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>RTX PRO 6000 S</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">49.3</td> <td style="text-align: right">65.9</td> <td style="text-align: right">37.0</td> <td style="text-align: right">39.4</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>A100 SXM4</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">60.6</td> <td style="text-align: right">51.1</td> <td style="text-align: right">49.3</td> <td style="text-align: right">N/A</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>CMP 170HX</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">51.5</td> <td style="text-align: right">46.2</td> <td style="text-align: right">45.9</td> <td style="text-align: right">N/A</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>A100 PCIe</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">38.4</td> <td style="text-align: right">36.1</td> <td style="text-align: right">N/A</td> <td style="text-align: right">N/A</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>The H100 led every completed context length.</strong> Its advantage narrowed from 20.5 tokens per second over the RTX PRO 5000 at roughly 16k tokens to 12.0 at roughly 32.8k tokens. The value ranking depends on whether you need the fastest first response or the lowest cost for a long-running session.</p> <h2 id="cost-per-million-decode-tokens"> <a href="#cost-per-million-decode-tokens" title="Cost per Million Decode Tokens">Cost per Million Decode Tokens</a> <a href="#cost-per-million-decode-tokens" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Cost per Million Decode Tokens">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Hourly price alone hides the useful comparison.</strong> Dividing the supplied hourly rate by decode throughput gives a rough rental cost for one million generated tokens. This ignores prompt processing, idle time, storage, data transfer, taxes, discounts, and failed or interrupted runs.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>GPU</th> <th style="text-align: right">Short-context rate</th> <th style="text-align: right">Approx. cost per 1M decode tokens</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>CMP 170HX</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">$0.420/hr</td> <td style="text-align: right">$2.27</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>RTX PRO 5000</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">$1.005/hr</td> <td style="text-align: right">$2.45</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>RTX 6000 Ada</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">$0.813/hr</td> <td style="text-align: right">$2.53</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>A100 SXM4</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">$0.680/hr</td> <td style="text-align: right">$3.12</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>A100 PCIe</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">$0.565/hr</td> <td style="text-align: right">$4.09</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>RTX PRO 6000 Max-Q</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">$1.507/hr</td> <td style="text-align: right">$4.98</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>H100 SXM</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">$2.693/hr</td> <td style="text-align: right">$5.57</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>RTX PRO 6000 S</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">$1.756/hr</td> <td style="text-align: right">$9.89</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>The CMP 170HX won this narrow arithmetic comparison.</strong> The RTX PRO 5000 and RTX 6000 Ada were close behind, and both provided more throughput than the CMP 170HX. For interactive use, the extra waiting time often matters more than the lowest token cost.</p> <h2 id="rent-buy-credits-subscribe-or-buy-hardware"> <a href="#rent-buy-credits-subscribe-or-buy-hardware" title="Rent, Buy Credits, Subscribe, or Buy Hardware?">Rent, Buy Credits, Subscribe, or Buy Hardware?</a> <a href="#rent-buy-credits-subscribe-or-buy-hardware" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Rent, Buy Credits, Subscribe, or Buy Hardware?">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>The right option depends on utilization and control requirements.</strong> A GPU rental is a variable compute bill. API credits are a variable model bill. A chat subscription is a fixed access fee with usage limits. Owned hardware is a capital purchase followed by electricity, cooling, maintenance, and depreciation.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Monthly budget and workload</th> <th>Recommended path</th> <th>Why</th> <th>Main compromise</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Under $10</strong></td> <td>Buy API credits or use a free local model</td> <td>Proves the workflow without idle GPU cost</td> <td>Less control over model hosting and rate limits</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>$10 to $30</strong></td> <td>API credits for occasional work, or a chat subscription for daily interactive use</td> <td>A subscription suits human chat, while credits suit scripts and measured calls</td> <td>Neither option gives a private 27B endpoint by default</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>$30 to $100</strong></td> <td>Rent an RTX 6000 Ada or RTX PRO 5000 only during active sessions</td> <td>This budget covers short research bursts and avoids ownership overhead</td> <td>The instance still needs setup, storage, monitoring, and shutdown discipline</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>$100 to $250</strong></td> <td>Rent a fast card for scheduled work, or test an owned workstation plan</td> <td>Sustained monthly usage starts to make utilization visible</td> <td>Rental availability and hourly rates change</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>$250 to $600</strong></td> <td>Compare a month of RTX PRO 5000 rental against a used or new local GPU</td> <td>This is the decision point for frequent private inference</td> <td>Hardware adds power, heat, support, and resale risk</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Above $600</strong></td> <td>Buy hardware only with high utilization, or reserve H100-class rental for burst work</td> <td>A mixed strategy avoids owning peak hardware for occasional demand</td> <td>Capital remains tied up in a single configuration</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>These bands are decision guides, not provider quotes. The benchmark rates show the key break-even issue: an H100 at $2.693 per hour costs about $64.63 for a continuous 24-hour day and about $1,941.00 for 30 days before storage or other charges. The RTX PRO 5000 at $1.005 per hour costs about $24.12 per day and $723.60 for 30 continuous days. A GPU rented only for active sessions has a different total from a GPU left running all month.</p> <h3 id="when-api-credits-win"> <a href="#when-api-credits-win" title="When API Credits Win">When API Credits Win</a> <a href="#when-api-credits-win" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="When API Credits Win">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>API credits win when usage is irregular, automation matters, and the task does not require a specific local model.</strong> Credits avoid GPU provisioning, model downloads, driver problems, and idle time. They also let you compare several hosted models before committing to hardware.</p> <p>API pricing differs by model and provider. OpenRouter’s model catalog is designed for comparing model context sizes, providers, and token pricing. Use the provider’s live calculator before comparing an API bill with this benchmark. A local GPU produces tokens without a per-token provider charge, but its rental hour continues while the instance waits.</p> <h3 id="when-a-subscription-wins"> <a href="#when-a-subscription-wins" title="When a Subscription Wins">When a Subscription Wins</a> <a href="#when-a-subscription-wins" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="When a Subscription Wins">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>A subscription suits a person who uses a hosted assistant every day.</strong> Claude’s current individual plans, for example, separate free, Pro, and Max access levels with different usage limits and features. A subscription is not the same as API access. It often gives a polished interface and bundled tools, while API credits give programmatic control.</p> <p>Choose a subscription when the work is mostly interactive writing, research, coding, or file review. Choose API credits when a script, application, or agent needs a metered endpoint.</p> <h3 id="when-vastai-wins"> <a href="#when-vastai-wins" title="When Vast.ai Wins">When Vast.ai Wins</a> <a href="#when-vastai-wins" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="When Vast.ai Wins">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Vast.ai wins when you need an open model, private runtime control, or a short burst of high throughput.</strong> You select the GPU, launch an instance, run Ollama, test a model, and shut the instance down when finished. This is a strong path for Qwen3.8 27B, abliterated variants, and other model files unable to fit a consumer laptop.</p> <p>The cost is operational work. You need to confirm the model is using the GPU, watch VRAM, protect the exposed service, preserve any required model files, and stop the instance after the run. A low hourly rate does not fix a forgotten instance.</p> <h3 id="when-buying-a-gpu-wins"> <a href="#when-buying-a-gpu-wins" title="When Buying a GPU Wins">When Buying a GPU Wins</a> <a href="#when-buying-a-gpu-wins" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="When Buying a GPU Wins">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Buying hardware wins after sustained utilization, stable model requirements, and a need for local control.</strong> The purchase removes rental availability risk and gives you a persistent environment. It also gives you the option to run private data without sending prompts to a hosted provider.</p> <p>The purchase price is only one part of the bill. Add the host system, power supply, storage, cooling, electricity, replacement risk, and the value of your setup time. A high-end card also sits idle during periods when API credits or a subscription would cost less.</p> <p>NVIDIA’s RTX 4090 reference specifications list 24 GB of memory, a 450 W total graphics power rating, and an 850 W minimum system power recommendation. This makes it a useful local-inference reference point, but its 24 GB capacity is below the 27B Q4_K_M configurations tested here. Check actual model memory use rather than assuming a card fits from the parameter count alone.</p> <h2 id="abliterated-and-uncensored-models"> <a href="#abliterated-and-uncensored-models" title="Abliterated and Uncensored Models">Abliterated and Uncensored Models</a> <a href="#abliterated-and-uncensored-models" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Abliterated and Uncensored Models">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Abliterated and uncensored model variants change the buying decision.</strong> Their appeal is often fewer refusal behaviors or fewer built-in restrictions. Their costs include weaker safety behavior, uncertain provenance, inconsistent prompt formatting, higher review needs, and possible license or acceptable-use limits.</p> <p>For these models, rent before buying. A one-day RTX PRO 5000 test at the supplied rate costs about $24.12 before other charges. This is enough to confirm model fit, GPU use, response quality, and operational risk.</p> <p><strong>Do not expose an uncensored model directly to the public internet.</strong> Put authentication, rate limits, logging controls, and network isolation in front of it. Avoid sending personal, confidential, or regulated data to a model source you have not reviewed.</p> <p>If the model becomes a daily tool, compare the monthly rental total with the full cost of an owned workstation. If usage is occasional, the rental remains easier to stop and replace.</p> <h2 id="benchmark-caveats"> <a href="#benchmark-caveats" title="Benchmark Caveats">Benchmark Caveats</a> <a href="#benchmark-caveats" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Benchmark Caveats">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>The missing results are part of the result.</strong> An <code>N/A</code> value means the run did not produce a valid measurement. It does not mean the GPU is slow by the amount implied by another card’s score.</p> <ul> <li><strong>The second H100 instance produced no valid benchmark set</strong> because the model download completed too late.</li> <li><strong>The 2x RTX 5060 Ti instance was excluded</strong> because Ollama loaded the model on the CPU instead of using the GPUs.</li> <li><strong>The Qwen3.8 27B 256k-token prompt was not completed.</strong> Its highest valid level was approximately 131k actual prompt tokens. Llama 3.1 8B marks 256k as unsupported because its context limit is 128K.</li> <li><strong>The requested <code>num_ctx</code> was not used as the ranking label.</strong> The final tables use actual <code>prompt_eval_count</code> values.</li> <li><strong>Two valid trials per context were summarized with the median decode result.</strong> This reduces the effect of one slow run, but it does not replace a larger test set.</li> <li><strong>The wrapper was simple by design.</strong> A tuned vLLM or llama.cpp deployment will produce a different ranking.</li> </ul> <h2 id="final-recommendation"> <a href="#final-recommendation" title="Final Recommendation">Final Recommendation</a> <a href="#final-recommendation" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Final Recommendation">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Start with an RTX 6000 Ada or RTX PRO 5000 rental.</strong> The RTX 6000 Ada is the budget choice when its $0.813 hourly rate is available. The RTX PRO 5000 is the stronger speed choice below H100 pricing. Use the H100 SXM for long prompts, demanding interactive latency, or a short benchmark window where time matters more than rental cost. For an 8B model, the CMP 170HX is worth testing when its lower hourly rate matters more than peak speed.</p> <p><strong>Do not buy a GPU after one successful test.</strong> Rent for a month of real workloads, record active hours, prompt lengths, concurrency, and model changes, then compare the rental total with the complete ownership bill. Buy hardware when the workload is frequent enough to keep the card busy and stable enough to justify the loss of flexibility.</p> <p>For occasional work, API credits or a chat subscription are simpler. For private local inference, open model experimentation, or abliterated model testing, Vast.ai provides a lower-commitment path than buying a workstation immediately. Use Llama 3.1 8B as the lower-memory baseline and Qwen3.8 27B when the larger model is the actual deployment target.</p> <h2 id="references"> <a href="#references" title="References">References</a> <a href="#references" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="References">#</a> </h2> <ol> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Vast.ai GPU cloud marketplace"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://vast.ai/"> <a href="https://vast.ai/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Vast.ai GPU cloud marketplace</a> </span> </li> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Vast.ai documentation: marketplace, instances, pricing, and rental types"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.vast.ai/"> <a href="https://docs.vast.ai/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Vast.ai documentation: marketplace, instances, pricing, and rental types</a> </span> </li> <li> <span itemscope
